levels.title: Software Engineering Fundamentals
levels.scope: become comfortable building, debugging, and deploying real software before adding LLMs. This is the engineering foundation for everything that follows.

modules.name: Python for AI Engineering

objectives.text: Write clean, idiomatic Python using functions, classes, modules, comprehensions, exceptions, and common standard-library utilities.
Reason confidently about core data structures: lists, tuples, sets, dictionaries, iterators, generators, and when to use each.
Use type hints, dataclass/Pydantic-style models, and static analysis to make interfaces explicit and catch mistakes earlier.
Understand mutability, references, scope, exceptions, context managers, and common Python failure modes.
Work with files, paths, environment variables, JSON, CSV, and basic serialization.
Understand synchronous vs asynchronous execution; use async / await to perform concurrent network/API calls without blocking.
Manage virtual environments and dependencies with uv; understand pyproject.toml, dependency locking, and reproducible environments.
Structure larger programs into modules and packages instead of writing everything in one script.
Write basic unit tests with pytest and learn to debug using stack traces, logs, and breakpoints.

modules.outcome: Build a small multi-file Python application that is typed, tested, dependency-managed, and capable of making concurrent external API calls.

modules.name: The Web: HTTP, REST & JSON

objectives.text: Understand the full HTTP request/response cycle: URL, method, headers, body, server processing, response, and status code.
Work with common methods such as GET, POST, PUT/PATCH, and DELETE, and understand idempotency at a practical level.
Understand important status-code families and common codes such as 200, 201, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 429, and 500.
Understand headers, query parameters, path parameters, request bodies, content types, and cookies at a practical level.
Produce, parse, validate, and manipulate JSON confidently.
Understand RESTful resource design and design clean endpoints for a simple application.
Understand authentication basics: API keys, bearer tokens, authorization headers, and why secrets should not be embedded in URLs or client code.
Use tools such as curl, Postman/Bruno, or Python HTTP clients to inspect and debug APIs.

modules.outcome: Read unfamiliar API documentation, construct requests manually, interpret responses, and design a sensible REST API.

modules.name: Building APIs with FastAPI

objectives.text: Build a FastAPI application with routes, path/query parameters, request bodies, and response models.
Use Pydantic models for validation, serialization, typed inputs, and typed outputs.
Understand dependency injection at a practical level for reusable application dependencies.
Return appropriate HTTP status codes and design consistent error responses.
Handle exceptions cleanly instead of leaking raw stack traces to clients.
Use FastAPI's automatically generated OpenAPI/Swagger documentation and understand how API schemas are derived.
Write synchronous and asynchronous endpoints and understand when each is appropriate.
Call external HTTP services from async endpoints without blocking the server.
Understand application startup/shutdown, configuration through environment variables, and basic middleware concepts.
Test endpoints using pytest and FastAPI's test client.

modules.outcome: Build a documented, validated, testable API that communicates with at least one external service.

modules.name: Data & Persistence Basics

objectives.text: Understand relational data modeling: tables, rows, columns, primary keys, foreign keys, relationships, and basic normalization.
Use PostgreSQL and write SQL for SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, filtering, sorting, grouping, joins, and basic aggregations.
Understand indexes conceptually and why query design affects performance.
Connect PostgreSQL to a Python/FastAPI application using a database driver or ORM.
Keep database credentials outside source code and manage configuration through environment variables.

modules.outcome: Build an API whose data survives application restarts and supports real CRUD operations backed by PostgreSQL.

modules.name: Git & Collaboration

objectives.text: Understand repositories, commits, branches, remotes, diffs, and the staging area.
Follow a practical workflow: branch → make changes → commit → push → pull request → review → merge.
Write useful commit messages and inspect history using Git tools.
Resolve merge conflicts confidently rather than avoiding them.
Understand .gitignore and prevent secrets, virtual environments, generated files, and local configuration from entering the repository.
Write a README that explains what the project does, how to install it, configure it, run it, test it, and call its API.
Understand basic collaboration concepts such as code review, pull requests, and protected main branches.

modules.outcome: Hand another developer your repository and have them understand, run, and contribute to it without needing you beside them.

modules.name: AI-Assisted Software Development

objectives.text: Understand the progression from autocomplete, to chat-based assistants, to coding agents that can read a repository, edit code, run commands, inspect the results, and iterate.
Distinguish AI-assisted engineering, where you direct and verify the work, from blind vibe coding, where you accept whatever is generated.
Use a coding agent such as Claude Code to explore an unfamiliar repository, implement targeted changes, and debug existing code.
Work the verification loop on every change: give context → generate → inspect the Git diff → test → debug → review → accept.
Understand the finite context window and give the minimum useful context for a task instead of pointing the agent at the entire repository.
Keep architecture, conventions, project commands, and testing instructions in a project instruction file such as CLAUDE.md, separate from temporary task context.
Practice spec-driven development: write the requirement and the specification, then review a plan before the agent changes the repository.
Turn prompts you retype into custom slash commands, and understand Skills as reusable capabilities with instructions, metadata, and examples that load only when needed.
Build skills for recurring work such as code review, test generation, documentation, refactoring, and repository-specific conventions.
Delegate specialized work to subagents such as a reviewer, tester, debugger, or researcher instead of forcing every responsibility into one context.
Connect the agent to systems outside the repository through MCP (Model Context Protocol): databases, APIs, developer tools, and documentation.
Use hooks to make formatting, linting, testing, and validation deterministic instead of asking a model to remember them.
Understand plugins as reusable bundles that package commands, skills, hooks, agents, and integrations together.

Understand that these skills transfer to any coding agent — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI — because the durable parts are context, specifications, planning, delegation, automation, and verification.

notes: Use AI aggressively for leverage and verify aggressively for correctness: a coding agent produces plausible but incorrect code as fast as it produces correct code, and correctness, architecture, security, and maintainability stay yours.
modules.tryIt: Build a small multi-file application with a coding agent — spec it, plan it, add one command or Skill, one subagent, one MCP integration, and one hook, then review every diff, run the tests, and fix at least one thing the agent got wrong.
modules.mentalModel: AI coding proficiency does not replace software engineering fundamentals. It multiplies them.
modules.outcome: Use a coding agent as an engineering collaborator across exploration, implementation, debugging, refactoring, and testing, with planning and verification around every meaningful change.

modules.name: Containers & Deployment

objectives.text: Understand the practical distinction between your application, its environment, and the machine running it.
Understand containers and images conceptually and why Docker improves reproducibility.
Write a Dockerfile, build an image, run a container locally, expose ports, and pass environment variables safely.
Understand image layers, .dockerignore, container logs, and common container startup failures.
Containerize a FastAPI application and connect it to its required configuration/services.
Deploy a service to a cloud/platform provider and expose it through a publicly reachable URL.
Configure production environment variables and secrets separately from local development.

modules.outcome: Take a service that works locally, containerize it, deploy it, and debug it when the production environment behaves differently.

modules.name: Capstone: Ship a No-AI REST Service

objectives.text: Build a complete application using Python + FastAPI + PostgreSQL + Git + Docker + deployment, with no LLM or AI dependency.
Design a small but realistic domain such as task management, bookmarks, expense tracking, inventory, notes, or support tickets.
Implement multiple REST endpoints with validated request/response schemas and persistent CRUD operations.
Include at least one external API integration and use async execution where appropriate.
Handle validation failures, missing resources, external-service errors, and unexpected server errors cleanly.
Add basic automated tests, configuration via environment variables, and useful application logging.
Maintain the project in Git with a clean repository structure and a README containing setup and usage instructions.
Package the service with Docker and deploy it to a publicly reachable URL.
Verify the deployed API using its OpenAPI docs, curl, or an API client.
Use a coding agent for meaningful parts of the build; "no-AI" means the deployed product needs no LLM, not that you code without AI tools.
Review every meaningful generated change through its Git diff before accepting it.
Validate generated code through tests, type checking, linting, logs, and manual API calls.
Explain the architecture and the important code paths yourself, without asking the coding agent.

Document one case where the coding agent produced an incorrect, incomplete, insecure, over-engineered, or otherwise suboptimal solution: what it proposed, why it was wrong, how you detected it, what you changed, and the engineering lesson you took from it.

modules.finalResult: a real service that another person can clone, run, test, call over HTTP, and inspect without any AI component hiding weak software-engineering fundamentals.

completionOutcomes: Write clean, typed, modular Python and debug it systematically.
Use async programming for network-bound workloads.
Manage dependencies and reproducible environments.
Understand HTTP requests, responses, REST APIs, authentication, and JSON.
Build validated, documented APIs with FastAPI.
Store and query application data using PostgreSQL and SQL.
Connect application code safely to a database.
Test application behavior rather than relying only on manual checks.
Work confidently with Git branches, commits, pull requests, and merge conflicts.
Structure a repository so another engineer can understand it.
Containerize an application with Docker.
Deploy a backend service to a public endpoint.
Use logs, errors, and traces to diagnose failures.
Ship a complete software service before an LLM enters the architecture.
Use coding agents for implementation, debugging, refactoring, testing, documentation, and repository exploration.
Give a coding agent the repository and task context it actually needs.
Use project-level instruction files such as CLAUDE.md to keep an agent aligned with the project.
Apply spec-driven development and planning before substantial AI-generated changes.
Encode repeated coding-agent work as reusable commands and Skills.
Delegate specialized tasks to subagents instead of overloading one context.
Connect a coding agent to external systems through MCP.
Use hooks and automation for deterministic engineering checks.
Review AI-generated code systematically using diffs and automated verification.
Detect hallucinated APIs, incorrect assumptions, security problems, architectural inconsistencies, and unnecessary complexity in generated code.
Understand and debug your own codebase even where AI helped write it.
Progression: Python → Async programming → HTTP/REST/JSON → FastAPI → PostgreSQL → Testing → Git collaboration → Agentic coding → Docker → Deployment → Ship a real backend.

levels.title: LLM 101
levels.scope: Build a strong mental model of how LLMs work, why they behave the way they do, and how to choose and use the right model for a task.

modules.name: What an LLM Actually Is

objectives.text: Understand what a Large Language Model actually does, with next-token prediction as the core idea and generation as a repeated predict → choose → append → repeat process.
Understand what an LLM is not: a database, search engine, deterministic program, or repository of stored answers.
Understand why the same underlying model can perform writing, summarization, translation, coding, question answering, and classification.
Build intuition for how capability improves through better data, more compute, larger models, and better training.

modules.tryIt: Give the same prompt multiple times and observe variation; predict the next word/token in simple sentences before asking the model.
modules.outcome: Explain an LLM simply: an LLM generates text by repeatedly predicting the most appropriate next token given the tokens it has already seen.

modules.name: Tokenization

objectives.text: Distinguish characters, words, and tokens; understand token IDs, why LLMs operate on tokens, and why different tokenizers can split the same text differently.
Explore tokenization of normal English, uncommon words, numbers, code, emojis, Hindi/Devanagari, and mixed Hindi-English text.
Connect tokenization to API pricing, context-window consumption, output length, latency, spelling difficulties, character-counting failures, and mathematical/numerical behavior.

modules.tryIt: Compare token counts for an English paragraph, its Hindi translation, source code, and a list of numbers.
modules.outcome: Explain why two texts with roughly the same number of words can have very different token counts and LLM costs.

modules.name: Inside an LLM: Embeddings, Attention & Transformers

objectives.text: Understand how token IDs become embeddings, what vectors represent conceptually, why concepts are represented numerically, and how representations change as they pass through transformer layers.
Understand what model parameters are and what sizes such as 8B, 70B, and 400B+ mean.
Understand why more parameters can increase capacity, while larger does not automatically mean better.
Understand attention through the intuition: a token looks at other relevant tokens in the context to build a better representation of what it means.
Build a high-level understanding of queries, keys, values, attention scores, transformer layers, and causal attention — without matrix mathematics.
Understand a dense model, where every parameter takes part in producing every token.
Understand a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model, where the feed-forward layers are split into many experts and a router selects only a few of them for each token.
Distinguish total parameters from active parameters, and understand why an MoE model with a very large total size can cost far less to run than a dense model of the same size.
Understand what MoE changes in practice: every expert still has to be held in memory, while the compute spent per token stays closer to that of a much smaller model.
Read MoE descriptions on model cards, such as "8x7B" or "total vs active parameters", and know what they tell you about speed, cost, and hosting requirements.

modules.tryIt: Inspect an attention visualization for a sentence such as “The animal didn't cross the street because it was tired” and reason about what "it" should attend to.
modules.mentalModel: Text → Tokens → Embeddings → Transformer layers + attention → Next-token probabilities
modules.outcome: Explain conceptually what happens between a token entering the model and the model producing next-token probabilities.

modules.name: How LLMs Learn

objectives.text: Understand pretraining, how enormous text datasets are used, why next-token prediction creates its own training signal, and what self-supervised learning means.
Understand how pretraining enables models to learn grammar, facts, patterns, concepts, relationships, coding syntax, and problem-solving patterns.
Explore memorization vs generalization, including why an LLM can sometimes answer questions it has never seen verbatim.
Understand the broad pipeline: Pretraining → Supervised Fine-Tuning → Preference / Reinforcement Training → Deployed Assistant.
Understand SFT, RLHF, RLAIF, preference optimization at a conceptual level, and safety tuning.
Connect post-training to why chat models follow instructions, answer conversationally, refuse certain requests, hedge, structure answers, and ask for clarification.

modules.tryIt: Compare a base model and an instruction-tuned model using identical prompts.
modules.outcome: Explain why a pretrained model may know a lot while still being a poor conversational assistant.

modules.name: How LLM Inference Works

objectives.text: Understand what happens after sending a prompt to an LLM API: Prompt → process input → predict token → generate token → repeat.
Distinguish prefill, where the model processes the input/context, from decode, where new tokens are generated one by one.
Understand input tokens, output tokens, time to first token (TTFT), tokens per second, and total latency.
Build intuition for KV caching and why the model does not need to recompute the entire conversation from scratch after every generated token.
Connect inference mechanics to latency, cost, long prompts, long outputs, and reasoning models.

modules.outcome: Explain why generating 2,000 output tokens usually takes much longer than generating 50 tokens even with the same input.

modules.name: The Context Window

objectives.text: Understand what the context window is and what can occupy it: system instructions, conversation history, user prompts, documents, examples, tool outputs, and generated content.
Distinguish context ≠ model knowledge ≠ long-term memory.
Understand what can happen with very long contexts: truncation, attention degradation, lost-in-the-middle effects, and context dilution.
Understand why a model supporting a huge context window does not mean it can use every token equally well.

modules.tryIt: Place an important fact near the beginning, middle, and end of a long document and compare retrieval performance.
modules.outcome: Decide whether a task needs a larger-context model or a better strategy for selecting what enters context.

modules.name: Sampling & Generation Parameters

objectives.text: Start from the model's next-token probability distribution and ask: which token should actually be generated?
Understand greedy decoding, temperature, top-p, top-k, maximum output tokens, stop sequences, and repetition/frequency/presence penalties where supported.

Understand task-dependent randomness: lower randomness for extraction, structured output, classification, and factual QA; higher randomness for brainstorming, creative writing, and diverse alternatives.
Understand that different model APIs expose different controls and that some reasoning models provide less direct control over traditional sampling parameters.

modules.tryIt: Run the same prompt at several temperature settings and compare consistency, creativity, and correctness.
modules.outcome: Choose sensible generation settings based on the task instead of changing temperature arbitrarily.

modules.name: Reasoning Models & Test-Time Compute

objectives.text: Understand why some models spend substantially more compute before producing an answer.
Build intuition for test-time compute, reasoning effort, thinking budgets, and internal reasoning tokens/compute.
Identify tasks where reasoning tends to help: difficult mathematics, complex coding, planning, multi-step logic, and constraint-heavy problems.
Identify tasks where it may be unnecessary: sentiment classification, simple extraction, rewriting, and straightforward summarization.
Understand the trade-off: more reasoning can improve quality but generally increases cost and latency.

Adapt prompting for reasoning models: move away from relying on “think step by step” and instead clearly state the goal, provide relevant context, specify constraints, and define what a good answer looks like.

modules.tryIt: Run the same problems through a fast general model and a reasoning model; compare accuracy, latency, and cost.
modules.outcome: Recognize when paying for extra reasoning compute is likely to be worthwhile.

modules.name: LLM Capabilities & Failure Modes

objectives.text: Understand common strengths: summarization, text transformation, extraction, classification, semantic understanding, coding, translation, brainstorming, working with unstructured information, and few-shot adaptation.

Understand common failure modes: hallucination, arithmetic mistakes, brittle reasoning, instruction-following failures, prompt sensitivity, context failures, outdated knowledge, nondeterminism, and confident incorrect answers.

Understand hallucination mechanistically: an LLM is trained to generate a likely continuation, not to independently verify that every generated statement is true, which makes fluent incorrect answers possible.
Adopt the engineering question: instead of “Can GPT do this?”, ask “How reliably does this model perform this task under the conditions of my application?”

modules.tryIt: Create 10 questions where the model knows the answer, probably does not know it, receives misleading information, or receives insufficient information; observe how confidence changes.
modules.outcome: Predict which tasks are naturally well suited to LLMs and which require additional safeguards.

modules.name: Understanding the Model Landscape

objectives.text: Understand closed/API models through trade-offs involving frontier capability, convenience, infrastructure, privacy, vendor dependence, and control.
Understand open-weight models through self-hosting, privacy, customization, infrastructure requirements, and operational complexity.

Understand the third path between them: managed platforms such as AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, and Azure AI Foundry serve both closed and open-weight models inside your own cloud account, and inference providers host open weights for you without any hardware of your own.
Learn other useful distinctions: small vs large, dense vs Mixture-of-Experts, general-purpose vs specialized, reasoning vs non-reasoning, and text-only vs multimodal.
Internalize the core principle: there is no universally best LLM; the best model depends on the workload.
Understand that a model's knowledge stops at its training cutoff, and that anything newer has to arrive through context, retrieval, or tools.
Track model versions and dated snapshots, and expect deprecations: the model behind a familiar name can change or be retired, so pin a version and re-test when it moves.
Check the license before building on an open-weight model, since permissive, restricted-use, and non-commercial terms differ in what you are allowed to ship.

modules.outcome: Compare two models using meaningful architectural, capability, and deployment differences rather than relying purely on leaderboard rank.

modules.name: Benchmarks & Leaderboards

objectives.text: Understand what a benchmark is: a fixed set of tasks with a fixed scoring method, used to measure different models against the same yardstick.
Recognize the benchmarks quoted on model cards — knowledge and reasoning tests such as MMLU and GPQA, coding tests, and mathematics tests — and know roughly what each one measures.
Read the main kinds of leaderboard: human-preference rankings such as LMArena/Chatbot Arena, aggregated capability/cost/latency dashboards, and open-model leaderboards.
Understand why a leaderboard rank rarely transfers to your application: different prompts, different tasks, averaged scores, and someone else's definition of a good answer.
Understand the pitfalls that inflate published scores: data contamination, saturated benchmarks, overfitting to public test sets, and favorable run configurations.
Use benchmarks and leaderboards for the one thing they do well — narrowing a crowded field to a shortlist — and then judge the shortlist on your own examples.

modules.tryIt: Shortlist three models from a leaderboard for a task you care about, then compare their published scores against how they perform on ten of your own examples.
modules.outcome: Read benchmark tables and leaderboards without being misled by them, and turn them into a shortlist rather than a decision.

modules.name: Choosing the Right Model

objectives.text: Evaluate models across eight dimensions:
Capability: Can it perform the task at all?
Quality: How reliably does it perform your specific task?
Latency: How quickly does it respond?
Cost: What will each request cost at your expected usage?
Context: Can it accommodate the required input?
Modalities: Do you need text, images, audio, or video?
Privacy & deployment: Can you use an external API, do you need a managed platform inside your own cloud, or do you require self-hosting?
Product features: Do you require structured outputs, function calling, tools, streaming, or caching?
Learn to critically read model cards, benchmark tables, pricing pages, context-window specifications, and API documentation.
Understand why benchmark scores alone should not determine model selection.
Follow the workflow: Define task → Identify requirements → Shortlist models → Test on your own examples → Measure quality → Measure latency → Measure cost → Inspect failures → Choose the model.

modules.outcome: Select models based on application requirements and empirical performance rather than popularity or leaderboard position.

levels.title: Working with LLM APIs (Orchestration)
levels.scope: turn individual LLM calls into reliable software workflows — messages, streaming, structured outputs, tools, multi-step orchestration, concurrency, failure handling, and observability. RAG and agents come later.

objectives.text: Call OpenAI/Anthropic SDKs; work with models, messages, system instructions, user/assistant roles, response objects, stop reasons, and usage metadata.
Understand that most LLM APIs are fundamentally stateless and learn to maintain conversation history explicitly.
Distinguish application state from information currently present in the model's context.
Manage API keys safely using environment variables, .env files, or secret managers; never expose server-side credentials in frontend code.
Inspect input/output tokens, request metadata, and model responses instead of treating the API as a simple prompt → string function.
Stream model output incrementally and render partial responses in a terminal or UI.
Understand TTFT, generation speed, perceived latency, and total latency.
Accumulate streamed events into a complete response and handle cancellations, interrupted streams, network failures, and incomplete generations.
Understand why orchestration libraries exist and what LangChain abstracts over raw provider SDKs.
Work with chat models, messages, prompt templates, output parsers, streaming, and model configuration.
Use LangChain with multiple model providers while understanding the underlying API calls it is making.
Learn the core composition model and build simple pipelines using prompts, models, parsers, and runnables.
Compare equivalent implementations using raw SDKs and LangChain to understand convenience vs abstraction overhead.
Keep the mental model that LangChain is an orchestration layer, not the LLM itself.
Generate schema-constrained outputs rather than relying on “please return JSON” prompting.
Define schemas using JSON Schema/Pydantic; work with required fields, optional fields, enums, lists, nested objects, and typed responses.
Implement structured outputs using both provider-native capabilities and LangChain abstractions.
Validate model outputs before passing them into application logic.
Distinguish syntactic validity from semantic correctness: valid JSON can still contain incorrect information.
Implement a generate → validate → accept / retry / repair / reject workflow for invalid outputs.
Understand that the LLM normally chooses a tool and generates arguments; your application executes the actual function.
Define tools using names, descriptions, parameter schemas, types, and required arguments.
Implement the full loop: user → LLM → tool request → execute tool → return result → LLM → final answer.
Work with tool-call IDs and correctly insert tool results back into the conversation.
Implement tool calling using provider APIs directly and understand how LangChain represents and executes tools.
Handle sequential calls, multiple calls to the same tool, parallel calls, and workflows where one tool result determines the next tool call.
Handle tool failures and malformed arguments instead of assuming every requested invocation is executable.
Design tools with precise names, clear descriptions, minimal parameters, strong types, and useful error responses.
Understand how ambiguous or overlapping tools can cause incorrect tool selection.
Avoid giving the model huge numbers of poorly differentiated tools or unnecessary arguments.
Treat model-generated arguments as untrusted input: validate types, values, permissions, and potentially destructive operations before execution.
Understand that tool descriptions themselves are part of the context the model uses to decide what action to take.
Move beyond prompt → model → answer and build workflows containing multiple LLM calls, tools, transformations, and application logic.
Implement common orchestration patterns: sequential pipelines, routing, conditional branches, and fan-out/fan-in.
Learn when to split a complex task into multiple specialized calls instead of using one enormous prompt.
Build some workflows manually to understand their control flow, then reproduce them using LangChain composition primitives.
Understand the distinction between application-controlled workflows and the more autonomous agentic systems introduced later.
Understand synchronous vs asynchronous API calls and when concurrency improves throughput.
Process many independent LLM requests concurrently rather than sequentially.
Use bounded concurrency so higher throughput does not immediately create rate-limit failures.
Apply async and batch execution using both provider SDKs and orchestration-layer abstractions.
Understand the trade-off between concurrency, throughput, latency, API limits, resource consumption, and cost.
Recognize common API failures: authentication errors, invalid requests, rate limits, server errors, network failures, timeouts, context-limit errors, and malformed model outputs.
Decide which failures should be retried and which should fail immediately; for example, authentication errors generally should not be retried while transient server errors may be.
Implement exponential backoff, jitter, maximum retry counts, sensible request timeouts, and graceful degradation.
Add model/provider fallbacks when appropriate, while understanding that fallback models may differ in quality and behavior.
Handle failures at both levels: LLM API failure and tool/API failure.
Understand where reliability logic should live: provider SDK, orchestration layer, or your application code.
Track model, input tokens, output tokens, latency, retries, errors, tool calls, and estimated cost for every request.
Treat a multi-step LLM interaction as a trace rather than an isolated API call.
Inspect which step caused a failure, which call consumed the most tokens, which tool was selected, and where latency accumulated.
Use callbacks/tracing to understand LangChain workflows and connect individual model and tool calls into a single execution trace.
Build enough logging and tracing that you can debug workflows without relying on scattered print() statements.
Understand that LangChain is one orchestration approach rather than a universal standard.
Explore LlamaIndex and how its abstractions and emphasis differ from LangChain.
Explore graph/state-machine style orchestration for workflows containing branches, loops, persistent state, and more complex control flow.
Get introduced to LangGraph as a graph-based approach for stateful LLM workflows.
Get introduced to DSPy as a more declarative approach where you specify desired input/output behavior rather than manually composing every prompt.
Compare orchestration approaches on development speed, abstraction overhead, debugging, portability, dependency complexity, state management, and control.
Develop the ability to choose between raw SDKs, LangChain, graph-based frameworks, LlamaIndex, DSPy, or a custom orchestration layer based on the application.
Build a conversational assistant that maintains history, uses system instructions, streams responses, and exposes at least 2–3 real tools/APIs.
Support sequential or parallel tool use where appropriate and validate all model-generated tool arguments.
Add structured outputs where useful, retry transient failures, enforce timeouts, and handle tool/API errors gracefully.
Record token usage, latency, retries, tool calls, and estimated cost so the entire workflow can be inspected.
Build the main implementation using LangChain while being able to explain the raw API/tool-call mechanics underneath it.
The final application should combine LLM + software + external tools + control flow + reliability, without relying on RAG or autonomous agents.

completionOutcomes: Call and understand modern LLM APIs rather than treating them as black boxes.
Maintain multi-turn conversation state and stream responses into a real application.
Use LangChain confidently while understanding what it abstracts from the underlying APIs.
Turn model outputs into validated typed data.
Give LLMs access to real software tools safely and implement the full tool-calling loop.
Build sequential, conditional, parallel, routed, and fan-out/fan-in workflows.
Process large numbers of calls concurrently.
Survive API failures, rate limits, and timeouts.
Measure token usage, latency, errors, tool activity, and cost.
Understand different orchestration approaches including raw SDKs, LangChain, LangGraph, LlamaIndex, and DSPy.
Decide when an orchestration framework is useful and which style best fits an application.
Build a complete production-style, tool-using LLM workflow.

levels.title: Prompt Engineering
levels.scope: design instructions that make LLM behavior more reliable and predictable. Context engineering comes later.

objectives.text: Structure prompts using instructions, context, input, constraints, examples, and output requirements.
Use system/user/assistant roles correctly and understand instruction priority.
Separate instructions clearly from user-provided or external data.
Know when a clear zero-shot instruction is sufficient and when examples are needed.
Design useful few-shot examples that demonstrate desired behavior and output format.
Understand how example quality, diversity, and ordering can affect results.
Distinguish few-shot prompting from fine-tuning.
Use reasoning-oriented prompting for complex logic, planning, mathematics, coding, and constraint-heavy tasks.
Know when extra reasoning is unnecessary for tasks such as extraction, classification, and rewriting.
Break complex tasks into clearer subproblems or intermediate steps.
Adapt prompting for reasoning models rather than relying blindly on “think step by step.”
Define application purpose, behavior, constraints, boundaries, and output expectations in the system prompt.
Separate stable application rules from task-specific user instructions.
Specify what the model should do when information is missing, ambiguous, or outside scope.
Add lightweight behavioral guardrails without turning the system prompt into an enormous rulebook.
Control response style, length, format, headings, labels, tables, and JSON through clear instructions and examples.
Know when prompting is enough and when structured-output/schema enforcement from Level 2 is more reliable.
Separate semantic instructions from programmatic format enforcement.
Diagnose failures caused by ambiguous instructions, conflicting constraints, poor examples, missing context, or unclear output requirements.
Build a small test set containing normal cases, edge cases, and known failures.
Compare prompt versions on the same examples instead of judging them from individual responses.
Reduce unnecessary output variance and regressions through systematic iteration.
Version prompts like code and track which prompt/model combination produced each result.
Compare prompt variants using quality, latency, token usage, and cost.
Remove unnecessary context and repeated instructions.
Understand prompt caching and structure reusable prompt prefixes to benefit from caching where supported.
Understand prompt injection and why external/user-controlled text should be treated as untrusted data.
Recognize attempts to override system instructions or extract hidden information.
Understand that prompt wording alone is not a security boundary; permissions and sensitive actions must be controlled by application code.
Leave deeper adversarial security and defenses for the later security level.
Choose one realistic task such as classification, extraction, support answering, or a domain-specific assistant.
Create a small test set and develop multiple prompt versions. Compare them on:
correctness,
instruction following,
output-format adherence,
consistency,
token usage,
latency/cost.
Select the final prompt based on measured performance rather than intuition.

completionOutcomes: Structure clear prompts using instructions, context, constraints, examples, and output requirements.
Decide when to use zero-shot, few-shot, or reasoning-oriented prompting.
Write effective system prompts.
Control model outputs while knowing when schemas are preferable.
Debug and improve prompts systematically using test cases.
Version and compare prompts based on quality, latency, and cost.
Recognize basic prompt-injection risks.
Treat prompt engineering as an iterative engineering process rather than a collection of tricks.

levels.title: RAG
levels.scope: build the retrieval layer that RAG depends on — ingestion, chunking, embeddings, vector search, and hybrid retrieval — then ground LLMs in external knowledge, improve retrieval quality, and learn the major RAG architectures used beyond a naive retrieve-and-generate pipeline.

modules.name: Data ingestion & document processing

objectives.text: Extract content from common sources such as PDFs, HTML, DOCX, and structured documents; understand when OCR is required.
Clean and normalize messy text while preserving useful document structure and metadata.
Handle duplicate documents, document updates, and incremental re-indexing.

modules.outcome: Convert a real-world document collection into clean, structured data ready for retrieval.

modules.name: Chunking strategies

objectives.text: Understand why documents must usually be split before embedding and retrieval.
Apply fixed-size, recursive, structural, and semantic chunking.
Reason about chunk size, overlap, boundaries, and metadata and how they affect retrieval quality.
Understand the trade-off between small precise chunks and larger context-rich chunks.

modules.outcome: Choose a sensible chunking strategy based on document structure and query type.

modules.name: Embeddings fundamentals

objectives.text: Understand embeddings as vector representations that capture semantic relationships between text.
Generate embeddings for documents and queries using an embedding model.
Understand dimensions, embedding model choice, multilingual/domain performance, cost, and latency trade-offs.
Understand that embeddings from different models/vector spaces generally cannot be mixed directly.

modules.outcome: Select and use an embedding model appropriate for a retrieval task.

modules.name: Similarity & semantic search

objectives.text: Understand cosine similarity, dot product, and Euclidean distance and how they are used to compare vectors.
Build a simple semantic-search system from scratch: query → embedding → similarity → top-k results.
Understand the difference between semantic similarity and exact keyword matching.
Explore common failure cases such as exact names, IDs, numbers, and rare terminology.

modules.outcome: Build semantic search without relying on a vector database and understand exactly what the database will later automate.

modules.name: Vector databases & ANN search

objectives.text: Store embeddings, documents, IDs, and metadata in a vector database such as pgvector or Qdrant.
Perform top-k vector search with metadata filtering.
Understand why brute-force search becomes expensive at scale and why Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search exists.
Build intuition for HNSW and IVF and their speed ↔ memory ↔ recall trade-offs without going deep into implementation mathematics.
Understand indexing, updates, deletes, and basic operational considerations.

modules.outcome: Build and query a scalable vector-search index over a real corpus.

modules.name: Sparse & hybrid retrieval

objectives.text: Understand traditional lexical retrieval and BM25, and why keyword search can outperform embeddings for some queries.
Compare sparse/BM25 retrieval with dense/vector retrieval.
Combine dense and sparse results using hybrid retrieval and techniques such as Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF).
Understand when hybrid retrieval helps, especially for queries containing names, technical terms, IDs, numbers, and exact phrases.

modules.outcome: Choose between dense, sparse, and hybrid retrieval rather than defaulting to vector search for every problem.

modules.name: Retrieval evaluation

objectives.text: Create a small set of queries with known relevant documents/chunks.
Understand top-k retrieval and calculate Recall@k.
Compare chunking strategies, embedding models, retrieval methods, and k using the same evaluation set.
Understand why retrieval quality should be measured independently before adding an LLM generator.

modules.outcome: Evaluate whether a retrieval system actually finds the information users need.

modules.name: Capstone: Build a Hybrid Search Engine

objectives.text: Ingest and clean a real document corpus, preserve useful metadata, chunk the documents, generate embeddings, and index them in a vector database.
Implement dense search + BM25 + hybrid retrieval, including metadata filters where useful.
Create a small evaluation dataset and compare approaches using Recall@k.
Deploy a simple search API/UI that returns the most relevant chunks for a user query.

modules.finalResult: a measurable retrieval system ready to become the retrieval component of a RAG application.

modules.name: RAG architecture & when to use it

objectives.text: Understand the core pipeline: query → retrieve → assemble context → generate answer.
Understand what RAG solves: private knowledge, frequently changing information, large knowledge bases, and source-grounded answers.
Know when not to use RAG: when the model already knows enough, the task is purely transformational, or the required knowledge can simply fit in context.
Distinguish retrieval failure from generation failure.

modules.outcome: Decide whether a problem genuinely needs RAG.

modules.name: Baseline RAG from scratch

objectives.text: Build a complete RAG pipeline manually using the retrieval system built earlier in this level.
Retrieve top-k chunks, assemble them into the prompt, and generate an answer grounded in the retrieved context.
Design prompts that instruct the model to answer from supplied evidence and avoid unsupported claims.
Handle cases where retrieval returns weak, irrelevant, or insufficient context.
Understand the effect of k, chunk ordering, and total context size on answer quality.

modules.outcome: Build a working RAG application without hiding the mechanics behind a framework.

modules.name: Reranking

objectives.text: Understand the two-stage pattern: retrieve many candidates → rerank → send the best chunks to the LLM.
Use cross-encoder or dedicated reranking models to reorder retrieved chunks.
Understand why reranking can improve relevance while adding latency and cost.
Compare retrieval with and without reranking and understand when reranking provides little benefit.

modules.outcome: Improve the quality of context sent to the LLM without simply increasing the number of retrieved chunks.

modules.name: Query transformation & RAG-Fusion

objectives.text: Understand why the user's original question is not always the best retrieval query.
Apply query rewriting, query expansion, multi-query retrieval, and HyDE.
Understand RAG-Fusion: generate multiple queries, retrieve for each, and combine rankings using techniques such as Reciprocal Rank Fusion.
Use multiple retrieval queries for ambiguous, multi-faceted, or poorly phrased questions.
Understand the trade-off between improved retrieval and additional LLM calls, latency, and cost.
Avoid query transformation when baseline retrieval already performs well.

modules.outcome: Transform difficult user questions into better retrieval queries.

modules.name: Grounding, citations & abstention

objectives.text: Generate answers grounded in retrieved evidence rather than unsupported model knowledge.
Attach claims to their supporting documents/chunks and produce useful source citations.
Understand that having citations is not the same as being grounded; the cited source must actually support the claim.
Detect insufficient evidence and respond with an appropriate “I don't know / insufficient information” instead of forcing an answer.
Keep retrieved evidence and model-generated synthesis clearly distinguishable.

modules.outcome: Produce answers that are traceable to evidence and can abstain when the evidence is insufficient.

modules.name: RAG variants & advanced patterns

objectives.text: Understand the progression from Naive RAG → Advanced RAG → adaptive/self-correcting RAG architectures.
Learn Self-RAG: retrieval is performed when needed and the model reflects on retrieved evidence and its generated response.
Learn CRAG (Corrective RAG): evaluate retrieved evidence and trigger corrective retrieval when the initial results are weak.
Learn Adaptive RAG: dynamically decide whether retrieval is required and which retrieval strategy should be used.
Understand iterative RAG, where retrieval and generation repeat until enough evidence has been gathered.
Understand multi-hop RAG, where answering requires several retrieval steps or combining evidence from multiple sources.
Learn Graph RAG: represent entities and relationships as a graph and retrieve/summarize information using graph structure rather than relying purely on vector similarity.
Build intuition for when Graph RAG is useful: highly connected knowledge, entity relationships, global questions, and information spread across many documents.
Compare advanced approaches on quality, complexity, latency, cost, and failure mode addressed rather than assuming more advanced RAG is always better.

modules.outcome: Recognize major RAG variants and choose an architecture based on why baseline RAG is failing.

modules.name: RAG with frameworks

objectives.text: Rebuild the manually created RAG pipeline using LlamaIndex or LangChain.
Work with framework abstractions for ingestion, indexes, retrievers, rerankers, query engines, and citations.
Implement common RAG improvements such as reranking and query transformation using framework components.
Compare the framework implementation with the hand-built version on control, development speed, debugging, and complexity.

modules.outcome: Use RAG frameworks productively while still understanding the retrieval and generation mechanics underneath them.

modules.name: Capstone: Deploy an Advanced RAG Application

objectives.text: Build a document Q&A application over a real corpus with ingestion, chunking, retrieval, generation, citations, and abstention.
Establish a baseline RAG pipeline and add at least one meaningful improvement such as reranking, query transformation, RAG-Fusion, hybrid retrieval, or an advanced RAG variant.
Handle weak retrieval and insufficient evidence gracefully.
Track latency, token usage, and cost across the pipeline.
Deploy the application as an API or simple user interface.

modules.finalResult: a complete RAG application that goes substantially beyond a basic retrieve → stuff context → generate demo.

completionOutcomes: Convert messy documents into retrieval-ready data.
Choose and tune an appropriate chunking strategy.
Understand and generate embeddings.
Build semantic search from first principles.
Use vector databases and understand ANN search conceptually.
Use metadata filtering effectively.
Understand BM25 and lexical retrieval.
Build dense, sparse, and hybrid retrieval systems.
Measure retrieval quality using Recall@k.
Improve retrieval based on evidence rather than intuition.
Decide when RAG is and is not the right architecture.
Build a complete RAG pipeline from scratch.
Understand how retrieval quality affects generation quality.
Improve retrieved context using reranking.
Improve difficult retrieval queries using rewriting, HyDE, multi-query retrieval, and RAG-Fusion.
Generate grounded answers with citations and appropriate abstention.
Explain and distinguish Naive RAG, Self-RAG, CRAG, Adaptive RAG, iterative RAG, multi-hop RAG, and Graph RAG.
Choose an advanced RAG architecture based on the failure mode of the baseline system.
Use RAG frameworks without treating them as black boxes.
Deploy a production-style RAG application.

levels.title: AI Agents
levels.scope: build systems where models can decide what to do next, use tools, maintain state, recover from failures, and collaborate with other agents. Planning · tools · MCP · memory · multi-agent · LangGraph.

modules.name: What is an agent?

objectives.text: Understand the basic loop: goal → decide → act → observe → repeat → finish.
Distinguish LLM call vs chain vs workflow vs agent, especially based on who decides what happens next.
Understand where agents are useful: open-ended, multi-step tasks where the execution path cannot be fully predetermined.
Know when a deterministic workflow is simpler, cheaper, and more reliable.
Understand the basic components of an agent: model, instructions, tools, state/memory, control loop, stopping conditions.

modules.outcome: Decide whether a problem genuinely requires an agent.

modules.name: ReAct, planning & reflection

objectives.text: Understand the ReAct pattern: the agent alternates between deciding what to do and acting on the environment.
Implement a simple agent loop manually before using a framework.
Understand step-by-step execution vs plan-first execution.
Break complex goals into subtasks and dynamically revise plans as new information appears.
Use reflection/self-correction when actions fail or results are insufficient.
Implement stopping conditions, maximum steps, and protection against repetitive loops.
Understand that more planning/reflection can increase quality but also latency and cost.

modules.outcome: Build an agent capable of solving a multi-step task without hard-coding its exact execution path.

modules.name: Tools for agents

objectives.text: Extend Level 2 tool calling into agentic tool use where the model repeatedly selects among available capabilities.
Design tools with clear names, descriptions, schemas, typed arguments, useful outputs, and useful error messages.
Improve tool selection and argument correctness.
Handle sequential, dependent, parallel, and repeated tool calls.
Handle tool failures and allow the agent to recover or choose an alternative.
Limit the size of tool results returned to the model so context does not become overwhelmed.
Separate read-only tools from consequential tools and add confirmation/permission checks where necessary.

modules.outcome: Give an agent useful capabilities without giving it uncontrolled access to the underlying application.

modules.name: MCP (Model Context Protocol)

objectives.text: Understand why MCP exists: provide a standardized way for AI applications to connect to external tools, resources, and prompts.
Understand the host → client → server architecture and the responsibility of each component.
Distinguish ordinary function calling from MCP: tool calling describes how a model requests an action, while MCP standardizes how external capabilities are exposed to AI applications.
Build an MCP server that exposes tools/resources from a real system such as a database, filesystem, SaaS application, or internal API.
Work with schemas, capabilities, errors, local/remote transports, and authentication.
Build/use an MCP client and connect it to one or more servers.
Understand permissions, trust boundaries, and the risk of connecting to untrusted MCP servers.

modules.outcome: Build a reusable MCP integration that can expose a real system to compatible AI applications.

modules.name: Memory basics

objectives.text: Distinguish conversation history, state, short-term memory, and long-term memory.
Implement short-term memory so an agent can retain information during a conversation or task.
Implement basic long-term memory using persistent stores or retrieval-backed memory.
Store useful facts, preferences, summaries, or previous outcomes instead of blindly preserving every message.
Retrieve relevant memories when needed rather than injecting the entire history into every request.
Understand basic memory operations: write → retrieve → update → forget.
Handle growing conversations through trimming or summarization.
Keep deeper context offloading/compression strategies for the later Context Engineering level.

modules.outcome: Build an agent that remembers relevant information during and across interactions.

modules.name: Multi-agent architectures

objectives.text: Understand why multiple agents may help when tasks require different tools, instructions, models, permissions, or areas of expertise.
Learn common patterns:
orchestrator → workers
sequential handoffs,
parallel specialists,
hierarchical supervisor/worker architectures.
Build an orchestrator that decomposes work and delegates tasks to specialist agents.
Pass useful state/context between agents and aggregate their outputs.
Handle worker failures, retries, reassignment, and escalation.
Understand common multi-agent problems: duplicated work, coordination overhead, context growth, conflicting results, latency, and cost.
Understand A2A as an interoperability approach for independently built agents and contrast it conceptually with MCP: MCP connects agents to tools/resources; A2A connects agents to agents.
Learn when multiple agents genuinely improve specialization and when one strong agent with several tools is preferable.

modules.outcome: Design multi-agent systems only when decomposition or specialization actually justifies the additional complexity.

modules.name: Building agents with LangGraph

objectives.text: LangGraph is positioned as a low-level orchestration framework/runtime for long-running, stateful agents.
Model agent execution using state, nodes, and edges.
Build nodes for model calls, tools, processing logic, and decisions.
Use conditional edges to dynamically determine the next action.
Implement loops for repeated tool use, retries, and iterative execution.
Add checkpointing/persistence so execution can survive interruptions.
Resume long-running agent runs rather than restarting them from scratch.
Add human-in-the-loop interrupts for actions requiring approval or intervention.
Inspect agent state to debug why a particular execution path was taken.
Understand when graph-based orchestration offers more control than a simple agent loop.

modules.outcome: Build a controllable, stateful, resumable agent with explicit execution logic.

modules.name: Sandboxed execution

objectives.text: Understand why model-generated Python, shell commands, or arbitrary programs should not execute directly inside the production application.
Run generated code inside isolated environments such as E2B, Modal, containers, or equivalent sandboxes.
Restrict filesystem, network, credentials, execution time, and compute resources.
Capture stdout, stderr, files, and errors and return only necessary results to the agent.
Understand the principle of reducing the blast radius when an agent can take executable actions.

modules.outcome: Give an agent code-execution capabilities without exposing the host system unnecessarily.

modules.name: Agent reliability, UX & failure recovery

objectives.text: Handle common failures: wrong tool selection, bad arguments, unavailable tools, repeated actions, incomplete plans, infinite loops, and context growth.
Define maximum steps, timeouts, retry budgets, cost/token budgets, and stopping conditions.
Make operations idempotent where possible so retries do not accidentally repeat real-world side effects.
Persist enough execution state to resume after interruption.
Add fallback actions and human escalation when the agent cannot continue safely.
Surface useful progress to users: current task, tool/action being performed, results, sources, and requests for approval.
Allow users to cancel, pause, resume, or redirect long-running work.
Avoid exposing unnecessary private reasoning while still making execution understandable.

modules.outcome: Build agents that fail predictably, recover gracefully, and keep the user informed and in control.

modules.name: Agent frameworks & libraries

objectives.text: After learning the primitives, implement the same small agent in several frameworks and understand what each one abstracts.
Low-level graph/state-based orchestration for long-running, stateful agents.
Strong fit when explicit control flow, persistence, loops, and human-in-the-loop behavior matter.
Build agents using Google's open-source ADK and explore its agent, session/state, tools, multi-agent, deployment, and A2A-related abstractions.
Understand its emphasis on building, debugging, evaluating, and deploying agent systems rather than merely wrapping an LLM call.
Build agents and collaborative Crews, and understand Flows for more controlled workflow-style orchestration.
Explore role-based multi-agent patterns and compare them with explicit graph orchestration.
Build Agents, Teams, and Workflows and understand the distinction between agent autonomy, team coordination, and deterministic workflows.
Explore its production/runtime layer and how agent systems can be exposed as services.
Build code-first agents using tools, handoffs, sessions, guardrails, tracing, and specialist agents.
Compare a lightweight SDK-style agent loop with graph-oriented or multi-agent-first frameworks.
abstraction level,
control over execution,
state/persistence,
multi-agent support,
tool integrations,
MCP/A2A support,
debugging/observability,
deployment,
vendor/model flexibility.

modules.outcome: Understand the agent-framework landscape and choose a framework based on architecture rather than popularity.

modules.name: Capstone: Build a Production-Style Agent

objectives.text: Choose one substantial project.
Option A · Research agent
Build:
Planner → Researcher → Analyst → Writer
with dynamic planning, tools, state, source tracking, retries, and optional specialist agents.
Option B · MCP-powered agent
Build an MCP server for a real service and an agent capable of using its tools/resources to complete multi-step tasks.
Option C · Coding/data agent
Build an agent that:
understands task → plans → writes code → executes in sandbox → inspects result/error → fixes code → returns output
Capstone requirements
at least 3 useful tools,
multi-step autonomous execution,
explicit state,
stopping conditions,
failure recovery,
logs/progress visibility,
at least one human approval point for consequential actions where appropriate,
implementation in one agent framework while being able to explain the underlying agent loop.

modules.finalResult: a real agent that demonstrates planning + tools + state + recovery + controlled autonomy, not merely an LLM wrapped in a while loop.

completionOutcomes: Distinguish chains, workflows, and agents.
Implement an agent loop from scratch.
Use ReAct, planning, and reflection appropriately.
Build robust tools for autonomous systems.
Build and consume MCP servers.
Implement short- and long-term agent memory.
Design orchestrator/worker and other multi-agent architectures.
Understand MCP vs A2A.
Build stateful agents using LangGraph.
Add checkpointing and human-in-the-loop control.
Execute model-generated code safely.
Design failure recovery and user-facing progress.
Work with LangGraph, Google ADK, CrewAI, Agno, and OpenAI Agents SDK and understand their different abstractions.
Choose between a deterministic workflow, single agent, or multi-agent system based on the actual problem.

levels.title: Context Engineering
levels.scope: manage the model’s limited context window deliberately — decide what enters, what stays, what gets compressed, and what gets moved outside.

modules.name: The context window as a resource

objectives.text: Treat context as a limited budget rather than “more is always better.”
Understand context rot, distraction, conflicting context, lost-in-the-middle, and token/cost growth.
Inspect what actually enters the model’s window and identify which parts are useful versus noise.
Allocate rough budgets across instructions, conversation history, retrieval, memory, tools, and working state.

modules.outcome: Diagnose when model degradation is really a context-management problem.

modules.name: Context selection & assembly

objectives.text: Assemble instructions + conversation history + retrieved knowledge + memory + tool definitions/results + application state deliberately.
Decide what should be always present, dynamically retrieved, summarized, or excluded.
Prioritize information based on relevance, importance, recency, and reliability.
Order and structure context so instructions, evidence, memory, and user data remain clearly distinguishable.
Avoid redundant, stale, contradictory, or irrelevant context.

modules.outcome: Construct the smallest useful context for the current model decision.

modules.name: Compression & compaction

objectives.text: Summarize growing conversation history while preserving goals, constraints, decisions, and unresolved work.
Compact large tool outputs before feeding them back into the model.
Apply rolling summaries and hierarchical summarization for long-running tasks.
Preserve exact structured information separately when summarization could lose important details.
Understand the trade-off between context reduction and information loss.

modules.outcome: Reduce context size without losing task-critical information.

modules.name: Memory & state offloading

objectives.text: Move information outside the active window using scratchpads, files, databases, memory stores, task state, and working notes.
Distinguish active context from information that can be stored externally and retrieved later.
Persist plans, completed steps, decisions, intermediate results, and important facts across long-running tasks.
Build note-taking agents that write useful information externally and recall it when required.
Understand the distinction between memory for remembering and offloading for freeing context space.

modules.outcome: Build systems that do not require the entire task history to remain inside the model’s context.

modules.name: Long-context strategies

objectives.text: Understand why large context windows do not eliminate context-engineering problems.
Manage lost-in-the-middle using better positioning, selective retrieval, and context restructuring.
Compare full-context stuffing, retrieval-over-history, summarization, hierarchical context, and selective loading.
Decide when to give the model more context versus retrieve only the relevant parts.

modules.outcome: Choose an appropriate strategy for very long documents, conversations, and agent runs.

modules.name: Tool context management

objectives.text: Understand that tool definitions and tool results also compete for context-window space.
Dynamically expose only the tools relevant to the current task where possible.
Summarize or filter large API/search/database outputs before returning them to the model.
Keep full tool results externally and retrieve details again when required.
Prevent long agent loops from accumulating unnecessary observations and tool output.

modules.outcome: Keep tool-heavy agents coherent without letting their action history overwhelm the context.

modules.name: Context caching & efficiency

objectives.text: Understand how repeatedly sending large static contexts affects cost and latency.
Structure stable instructions and reusable context to benefit from prompt/context caching where supported.
Separate stable context from rapidly changing task state.
Reduce redundant tokens while preserving useful information.
Measure token usage, cache utilization, latency, and cost rather than optimizing blindly.

modules.outcome: Make large-context applications more efficient without sacrificing quality.

modules.name: Capstone: Context-Managed Long-Horizon Agent

objectives.text: Take a tool-using agent from Level 5 and run it through a long task where naive context accumulation causes degradation.
Define an explicit context budget and dynamically decide what to keep, retrieve, compress, offload, or discard.
Add history compaction, external state, selective memory retrieval, and tool-output compression.
Preserve the original goal, constraints, completed work, and pending tasks across a long execution.
Compare the context-managed version against a naive “keep everything” implementation on coherence, token usage, latency, and cost.

modules.finalResult: an agent that stays useful across a long, tool-heavy session because its context is actively managed.

completionOutcomes: Diagnose context-related failures.
Treat the context window as a finite engineering resource.
Select and prioritize what deserves to enter the window.
Assemble instructions, retrieval, memory, state, and tool outputs effectively.
Compress long histories without losing critical information.
Offload state and working knowledge outside the active context.
Choose between long-context stuffing, retrieval, summarization, and selective loading.
Manage context growth in tool-heavy agents.
Use caching and context reduction to control latency and cost.
Build long-running agents that continuously keep, retrieve, compress, offload, and discard information.

levels.title: LLM Evaluations
levels.scope: Design, execute, and automate comprehensive evaluations for Large Language Models and AI applications to ensure quality, safety, and reliability in production environments.

modules.name: Introduction to LLM evaluations

objectives.text: Understand the pitfalls of “vibe testing” by examining real-world failure case studies like Air Canada.
Navigate the differences between deterministic software testing and probabilistic LLM systems.
Distinguish between evaluating core foundation model capabilities and testing complete application workflows.
Implement an end-to-end evaluation process covering task definition, criteria, datasets, execution, analysis, and iteration.

modules.outcome: Understand the foundational need for and workflow of LLM evaluations compared to traditional software testing.

modules.name: Evaluation methods & paradigms

objectives.text: Categorize evaluation execution mechanisms into Programmatic, Human, and LLM-as-a-Judge approaches.
Understand reference-based vs reference-free evaluation.
Determine when a Golden Dataset answer key is required versus when evaluation can rely entirely on LLM judgment.
Choose the appropriate evaluation method based on whether the target behavior is deterministic, semantic, subjective, or operational.

modules.outcome: Select the appropriate evaluation execution method and paradigm for a given LLM testing scenario.

modules.name: Offline vs online evaluations

objectives.text: Use offline evaluation suites for pre-release testing, version comparison, experimentation, and preventing performance regression.
Identify post-deployment production risks including unexpected inputs, emergent systematic failures, changing user behavior, and data drift.
Differentiate automatically captured system metrics such as latency, token usage, and errors from LLM-computed quality metrics such as hallucination or relevance.
Implement a continuous online evaluation pipeline through production logging, sampling, dashboarding, and alerting.
Feed important production failures back into the offline evaluation dataset.

modules.outcome: Design a dual-layer evaluation strategy that catches regressions before release and monitors quality after deployment.

modules.name: Model evaluations & benchmarking

objectives.text: Explore core LLM capabilities such as knowledge, reasoning, mathematics, coding, instruction following, long-context understanding, multimodal capability, safety, and tool use.
Analyze the anatomy of a benchmark through its dataset, prompts, run configuration, scoring method, and result aggregation.
Understand how public leaderboards compare foundation models.
Identify benchmark pitfalls including data contamination, score saturation, benchmark overfitting, and configuration gaming.

modules.outcome: Critically assess public LLM benchmarks and understand how core model capabilities are formally measured.

modules.name: The evolution of knowledge benchmarks

objectives.text: Trace the progression from benchmarks such as MMLU and TruthfulQA toward harder tests of knowledge and factual reliability.
Understand the use of human exams in benchmarks such as AGIEval to compare human and model capabilities.
Explore harder benchmarks such as GPQA, MMLU-Pro, SimpleQA, and Humanity's Last Exam.
Understand why benchmarks continually become harder as frontier models saturate older datasets.

modules.outcome: Understand the progression of knowledge benchmarks and select appropriate tests for increasingly capable models.

modules.name: Custom model evaluations

objectives.text: Move beyond public benchmarks and evaluate models on the actual task your application needs to solve.
Use leaderboards and aggregation platforms to shortlist candidate models based on capability, latency, context, and cost.
Build a custom evaluation dataset for a real task such as Text-to-SQL.
Compare shortlisted models using the same inputs, prompts, parameters, and scoring criteria.
Estimate API usage and token costs and use techniques such as prompt caching where appropriate.
Select the model that offers the best task-specific quality / latency / cost trade-off, rather than simply choosing the highest-ranked general model.

modules.outcome: Evaluate and select the most capable and cost-effective foundation model for a specific application.

modules.name: Building an eval suite & regression testing

objectives.text: Structure evaluations across component level, pipeline level, and application level depending on what is being tested.
Maintain versioned test cases, evaluation configurations, prompts, models, and results.
Track experiments and compare new versions against established baselines.
Build automated CI/CD quality gates so changes cannot ship when important metrics regress.
Create a self-improving loop by adding edge cases and failures discovered in production back into the offline golden dataset.
Track quality together with latency and cost so improvements in one area do not silently damage another.

modules.outcome: Build an automated evaluation suite that prevents regressions and improves continuously from real-world usage.

modules.name: RAG Evals

objectives.text: Evaluate a RAG system at component, pipeline, application, and safety levels, rather than treating it as one black-box system.
Evaluate the retriever independently to determine whether it finds the information required to answer the question.
Diagnose cases where the retriever completely misses the relevant context or retrieves excessive irrelevant/noisy chunks.
Measure retrieval effectiveness using metrics such as Contextual Recall, Contextual Precision, Recall@k, and other ranking-aware metrics where appropriate.
Generate or curate relevant chunks and ideal answers for a Golden Dataset through hand-authoring, LLM-assisted generation, or tools such as DeepEval's synthetic-data generators.
Evaluate the generator independently by providing known-good context and checking whether it produces faithful and relevant answers.
Detect unfaithful claims, irrelevant answers, missing information, and misuse of provided context.
Implement component tests using frameworks such as DeepEval or RAGAS while understanding what each metric actually measures.
Evaluate the complete retrieval → context → generation pipeline.
Measure the RAG Triad:
Contextual Relevancy
Faithfulness
Answer Relevance
Understand how individually strong components can still interact poorly when connected.
Diagnose cases such as high retrieval precision but low overall contextual relevance or poor downstream answers.
Determine whether the root failure lies in retrieval, assembled context, or generation.
Evaluate the RAG system from the actual user's perspective rather than only testing internal components.
Measure whether the final answer is factually correct given the available evidence.
Evaluate completeness: does the answer address all important parts of the user's request?
Evaluate application-specific requirements such as tone, style, persona, format, citation behavior, and instruction following.
Track operational metrics including latency, token usage, cost per query, and error rates alongside quality.
Evaluate whether the system produces harmful, illegal, dangerous, biased, or otherwise disallowed responses.
Test whether sensitive PII such as contact details, credentials, or payment information is appropriately protected or redacted.
Test direct and indirect prompt injection, including malicious instructions hidden inside retrieved documents.
Test jailbreak attempts intended to bypass application guardrails.
Evaluate whether retrieved malicious or misleading content can manipulate the model into leaking data or ignoring application instructions.

modules.outcome: Evaluate a RAG application comprehensively across retrieval quality, generator behavior, pipeline interaction, user-facing quality, operational performance, and safety.

modules.name: Agent Evals

objectives.text: Evaluate agentic systems at the level of decision-making, trajectories, tool usage, task completion, recovery, and safety.
Understand why evaluating only the final answer is insufficient when an agent autonomously decides how to complete a task.
Evaluate whether the agent chooses the correct tool for a given situation.
Test whether the agent generates accurate and properly formatted tool arguments.
Evaluate the sequence of actions taken by the agent and whether the trajectory is appropriate for the task.
Detect unnecessary tool calls, redundant actions, loops, incorrect ordering, and premature termination.
Measure overall task-completion success rate for complex multi-step user requests.
Introduce tool failures, malformed results, unavailable services, missing information, and unexpected intermediate states.
Evaluate whether the agent notices failure and chooses an appropriate recovery strategy.
Test whether it can retry, select an alternative tool, revise its plan, or escalate appropriately.
Measure successful recovery rather than only measuring success in ideal conditions.
Test whether agents attempt unauthorized or destructive actions.
Evaluate human-approval gates and permission boundaries around consequential actions.
Test agent resistance to direct and indirect prompt injections designed to hijack its tool usage.
Attempt to manipulate an agent into revealing secrets, exceeding permissions, or using tools outside the intended scope.
Use relevant cybersecurity benchmarks where appropriate to assess dangerous capabilities such as exploitation, reverse engineering, or other high-risk computer-use behavior.
Track both outcome quality and execution efficiency through steps, latency, tool calls, token usage, and cost.

modules.outcome: Systematically evaluate whether an agent makes good decisions, uses tools correctly, completes tasks efficiently, recovers from failures, and remains within its security boundaries.

completionOutcomes: Design end-to-end evaluation workflows for both offline testing and online production monitoring.
Choose between programmatic, human, reference-based, reference-free, and LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation methods.
Understand and critically interpret public LLM benchmarks.
Build custom model evaluations for specific application tasks.
Create versioned evaluation suites and automated regression testing.
Evaluate RAG systems across retriever, generator, pipeline, application, operational, and safety dimensions.
Measure RAG metrics such as contextual recall, contextual precision, contextual relevance, faithfulness, and answer relevance.
Evaluate agents across tool selection, argument correctness, trajectories, task completion, recovery, efficiency, and safety.
Build production feedback loops that continuously enrich offline evaluation datasets.
Use evaluations as an engineering system for improving AI applications rather than as a one-time benchmark exercise.

levels.title: AI Security
levels.scope: secure LLM, RAG, and agent systems against model-specific attacks, unsafe actions, data leakage, and regulatory risk.

modules.name: AI threat model

objectives.text: Understand how the attack surface changes when models can process untrusted content, access private data, call tools, and take actions.
Identify trust boundaries across prompts, retrieved data, tools, memory, model outputs, and external systems.
Treat model-generated outputs and actions as untrusted until validated.

modules.outcome: Threat-model an LLM application before adding defenses.

modules.name: Prompt injection & data exfiltration

objectives.text: Distinguish direct prompt injection from indirect injection hidden inside documents, web pages, emails, retrieved chunks, or tool outputs.
Understand attacks that attempt to override instructions, manipulate tools, expose private context, or redirect an agent's objective.
Understand the dangerous combination of untrusted input + powerful tools/private data + an exfiltration path.
Defend using instruction/data separation, least privilege, authorization checks, restricted tools, confirmation gates, and output validation.
Understand why prompting the model to “ignore malicious instructions” is not a sufficient security boundary.

modules.outcome: Build applications that remain safe even when malicious instructions reach the model.

modules.name: Jailbreaks, guardrails & moderation

objectives.text: Distinguish jailbreaks from prompt injection and recognize common jailbreak patterns.
Add input and output guardrails, moderation, validation, and policy checks.
