Understand the limitations of model-based guardrails and why multiple layers of defense are required.
Test guardrails against adversarial and obfuscated inputs instead of only normal requests.

modules.outcome: Reduce unsafe model behavior without relying on a single defensive prompt.

modules.name: Agent & tool security

objectives.text: Apply least privilege so agents only receive the tools and permissions required for the task.
Separate read-only actions from consequential actions such as sending messages, modifying records, deleting data, purchasing, or executing code.
Validate tool selection, arguments, permissions, and outputs independently of the LLM.
Add human approval for sensitive or irreversible operations.
Limit agent steps, runtime, cost, and tool usage to prevent runaway execution.
Sandbox model-generated code and treat generated SQL, commands, URLs, or API calls as untrusted.

modules.outcome: Give agents useful autonomy without giving them unrestricted control over real systems.

modules.name: RAG & knowledge security

objectives.text: Treat retrieved documents as untrusted data, not trusted instructions.
Understand retrieval poisoning and malicious instructions hidden inside indexed documents.
Enforce document-level permissions so users retrieve only information they are authorized to access.
Prevent cross-user or cross-tenant data leakage from vector stores and memory systems.
Preserve source/provenance information for retrieved content.

modules.outcome: Secure the knowledge layer underneath a RAG application.

modules.name: Data privacy, PII & secrets

objectives.text: Identify sensitive data including PII, credentials, financial information, private conversations, and confidential business data.
Detect, redact, mask, or minimize sensitive information before sending it to models when appropriate.
Avoid unnecessarily storing sensitive data in prompts, logs, traces, memories, vector stores, or evaluation datasets.
Understand data retention, deletion, residency, access control, and third-party model-provider considerations.
Use the controls that make regulated deployments possible: private connectivity to the model endpoint, no public egress, and contractual zero-retention or no-training terms.
Protect secrets so they are never unnecessarily exposed to the model.

modules.outcome: Minimize the amount of sensitive information exposed throughout an AI system.

modules.name: Red teaming AI systems

objectives.text: Build adversarial tests for prompt injection, jailbreaks, malicious documents, tool misuse, data extraction, and unsafe agent actions.
Test RAG systems by injecting malicious content into retrievable documents.
Test agents by attempting to make them exceed permissions, misuse tools, reveal secrets, or enter loops.
Turn discovered vulnerabilities into permanent security regression tests.
Track measures such as attack-success rate, sensitive-data leakage, and unsafe-action rate where useful.

modules.outcome: Test defenses adversarially instead of assuming they work.

modules.name: Responsible AI & governance

objectives.text: Understand core concerns around hallucination, bias/fairness, transparency, accountability, and human oversight.
Document intended use, known limitations, important risks, evaluations, and human-control mechanisms.
Understand the practical implications of relevant regulations such as the EU AI Act and India's DPDP framework.
Maintain auditability through model/prompt versions, logs, approvals, and evaluation records.

modules.outcome: Recognize when an AI application creates governance or compliance obligations.

modules.name: Capstone: Red-Team & Secure an Agentic RAG App

objectives.text: Take an application built in earlier levels and attack it using:
direct and indirect prompt injection,
malicious retrieved documents,
jailbreak attempts,
private-data extraction,
tool misuse,
unauthorized actions.
Then add:
least-privilege tools,
permission checks,
guardrails,
PII/secrets protection,
approval gates,
sandboxing,
security regression tests.

modules.finalResult: an AI system designed to remain safe even when the model makes a bad decision or receives malicious input.

completionOutcomes: Threat-model LLM, RAG, and agent applications.
Defend against direct and indirect prompt injection.
Implement practical guardrails and moderation.
Secure agent tools using least privilege and human approval.
Protect RAG systems against malicious or unauthorized knowledge.
Protect PII, secrets, and user data.
Red-team AI systems and turn attacks into regression tests.
Understand the basic governance obligations surrounding production AI.
Design around the principle that the model itself is not a security boundary.

levels.title: AI System Design
levels.scope: design a complete production AI application and defend every architectural choice across quality, latency, cost, reliability, and user experience.

modules.name: The AI system design framework

objectives.text: Start from the use case, success criteria, constraints, traffic, latency requirements, quality requirements, privacy, and cost budget.
Decide deliberately between prompting, RAG, agents, fine-tuning, or combinations of them.
Reason about the central trade-offs: quality ↔ latency ↔ cost, plus complexity and reliability.
Establish a simple baseline before introducing sophisticated architecture.

modules.outcome: Turn a product requirement into a defensible AI architecture rather than starting with a favorite technology.

modules.name: Context & knowledge architecture

objectives.text: Decide what knowledge should come from model knowledge, prompt/context, RAG, memory, or external tools.
Design the full context pipeline: ingestion → retrieval → reranking → context assembly → generation.
Combine vector, keyword, graph, and other retrieval approaches where justified.
Handle freshness, updates, access control, scale, and source provenance.
Decide what information should be retrieved dynamically versus kept permanently in the model's context or external state.

modules.outcome: Design the knowledge layer that supplies the model with the right information at the right time.

modules.name: Model routing & gateways

objectives.text: Understand the role of a model gateway as the abstraction between application code and model providers.
Route requests based on task type, capability, latency, context length, cost, modality, or risk.
Build model cascades where cheaper/faster models handle easy requests and stronger models handle difficult ones.
Add model/provider fallbacks and understand the quality risks introduced by switching models.
Centralize authentication, usage tracking, retries, rate limits, and provider abstraction where appropriate.

notes: This maps particularly closely to Huyen’s architecture step of adding a model router and gateway.
modules.outcome: Avoid designing applications around a single hard-coded model.

modules.name: Latency & inference optimization

objectives.text: Break latency into components such as retrieval, TTFT, model generation, tool calls, and network overhead.
Use streaming to improve perceived latency.
Parallelize independent operations and avoid unnecessary sequential LLM calls.
Understand when smaller/faster models can replace larger models.
Apply prompt/context reduction, batching, and inference-service optimizations where appropriate.
Reason about throughput, latency, and utilization at scale.

notes: Inference performance and both model- and service-level optimization are major topics in the book’s inference optimization chapter.
modules.outcome: Identify where an AI application is slow and choose the appropriate optimization instead of simply upgrading infrastructure.

modules.name: Caching architecture

objectives.text: Understand the different caches available in an AI system: exact-response caching, prompt/context caching, retrieval caching, and semantic caching.
Decide what is safe to cache and define appropriate expiration/invalidation strategies.
Use semantic caching when different queries can reasonably share an answer.
Understand the trade-off between freshness, quality, latency, and cost.
Measure actual cache hit rate and savings rather than assuming caching helps.

notes: Caching is another explicit step in Huyen’s production AI architecture.
modules.outcome: Use caching as an architectural optimization rather than an afterthought.

modules.name: Reliability, guardrails & graceful degradation

objectives.text: Design for model failures, provider outages, tool failures, rate limits, malformed outputs, and retrieval failures.
Add timeouts, retries, fallbacks, circuit breakers, queues, and rate limits where appropriate.
Place guardrails at important system boundaries rather than relying entirely on the model.
Design graceful degradation: simpler model, reduced functionality, cached answer, human escalation, or explicit inability to complete the request.
Use human approval for high-risk or irreversible actions.
Define service-level expectations for availability, latency, and quality.

modules.outcome: Design a system that remains useful when individual AI components fail.

modules.name: AI pipeline orchestration

objectives.text: Design the end-to-end flow between retrieval, models, tools, agents, guardrails, caches, and external systems.
Decide which decisions should be deterministic and which should be delegated to the model.
Choose between synchronous execution, asynchronous jobs, queues, and long-running agent workflows.
Avoid unnecessary agentic complexity when a deterministic pipeline is sufficient.
Define clear component boundaries so individual parts can be changed, evaluated, and scaled independently.

notes: Pipeline orchestration and agent patterns both appear explicitly in the book’s final architecture chapter.
modules.outcome: Turn individual AI components into a coherent production system.

modules.name: Monitoring, feedback & continuous improvement

objectives.text: Connect evals, traces, operational metrics, and user feedback into the production architecture.
Monitor quality, latency, cost, errors, retrieval behavior, tool usage, and model/provider performance.
Capture explicit feedback such as ratings as well as useful implicit behavioral signals.
Turn production failures and user feedback into new evaluation cases.
Version models, prompts, retrieval configurations, and application changes so regressions can be traced.
Understand the loop: deploy → observe → collect feedback → evaluate → improve → redeploy.

notes: Huyen’s final chapter explicitly treats monitoring/observability and user-feedback design as parts of the AI engineering architecture.
modules.outcome: Design AI products that improve from real-world usage rather than remaining static after launch.

modules.name: AI system design case studies

objectives.text: Whiteboard several systems end-to-end and defend the choices.
Design around:
RAG and fresh knowledge,
citations,
model routing,
caching,
escalation to humans,
latency and cost constraints.
Design around:
large codebase context,
retrieval,
tool/code execution,
model selection,
sandboxing,
long-running tasks.
Design around:
search and retrieval,
planning,
parallel tool calls,
context management,
long-running execution,
citations,
cost budgets and failure recovery.
For each case, reason about requirements → baseline → architecture → bottlenecks → failure modes → scaling → trade-offs.

modules.outcome: Defend architectural decisions rather than merely draw boxes and arrows.

modules.name: Capstone: AI System Design Document

objectives.text: Choose a substantial AI product and produce a complete design covering:
requirements and success criteria,
expected traffic and constraints,
high-level architecture,
model choice and routing,
context/RAG architecture,
tools/agents where required,
caching strategy,
latency and cost budget,
reliability and fallback strategy,
security/guardrails,
evaluation and monitoring,
user-feedback loop,
scaling strategy.
Include an architecture diagram and explicitly justify the major trade-offs and alternatives rejected.

modules.finalResult: a design you could defend in an AI system-design interview or an engineering architecture review.

completionOutcomes: Translate product requirements into an AI system architecture.
Decide between prompting, RAG, agents, and fine-tuning.
Design context and retrieval architecture.
Build model routing, gateways, cascades, and fallbacks.
Optimize inference for latency, throughput, and cost.
Design appropriate caching layers.
Build for failures and graceful degradation.
Decide what should be deterministic versus agentic.
Integrate monitoring, evals, and user feedback into the architecture.
Reason about the entire application rather than optimizing individual AI components in isolation.
Whiteboard and defend a production AI system end-to-end.

levels.title: LLMOps: From Development to Production
levels.scope: Launch, test, watch, and protect Large Language Model apps in the real world while managing changing outputs, prompt updates, and the special behaviors of RAG and Agent systems.

modules.name: Foundations of LLMOps

objectives.text: Define exactly what LLMOps is: the organized process of building, testing, watching, and running Large Language Model applications in the real world.
Explain why LLMOps is its own special field and how it is different from regular MLOps.
Compare Model LLMOps (which means training, fine-tuning, and hosting raw AI models) with Application LLMOps (which means building and running useful apps on top of existing AI models).

Look at the Model LLMOps lifecycle—gathering huge amounts of data, updating model weights, and managing massive servers—and understand why we chose to focus on Application LLMOps instead, since most teams today build apps rather than make their own models from scratch.
Map the complete journey of an LLM app from early building stages to putting it live and watching its performance.
Show how the daily running of a RAG app is different from an Agentic app.
Give a big-picture view of the whole LLMOps toolkit, including how we access models, check quality, track errors, keep things safe, and update code automatically.
Understand the two main projects (a RAG app and an Agentic app) that we will build and manage during this course.

modules.outcome: Understand the full journey of an LLM application and the complete LLMOps toolkit before writing any code.

modules.name: Application development

objectives.text: Build a RAG app that reads documents, breaks them into pieces, stores them, and connects them to an LLM to answer questions.
Build an Agent app that uses tools, plans steps, remembers past actions, and works on its own.
Use basic tools like LangChain for RAG, LangGraph for Agents, Chroma for storage, and OpenAI or Anthropic models.

modules.outcome: Set up the basic RAG and Agent apps that we will improve and put online in later steps.

modules.name: Evaluation

objectives.text: Create test question-answer pairs automatically using DeepEval instead of typing them out by hand.
Run a full test on both apps and save the starting scores in MLflow before changing any code.
Score the RAG app on how truthful and exact it is using AI-as-a-judge tools.
Score the Agent app on whether it picks the right tools, finishes the job, and takes logical steps.
Set up automatic alarms to catch if new changes break the app.

modules.outcome: Measure the quality of your LLM apps automatically without needing humans to check every answer.

modules.name: Experiment tracking & prompt versioning

objectives.text: Save and manage different versions of prompts using Langfuse so apps can pull them when running.
Label prompt versions for different stages like testing and live production.
Keep track of RAG settings (like chunk size) and Agent settings (like tools) as recorded MLflow experiments.
Track Metrics and artifacts along with the parameters.
Compare different prompt versions side-by-side in a dashboard to see how changes affect the output.

modules.outcome: Keep a clear, organized history of your prompts and app settings so you can easily repeat success.

modules.name: Guardrails & output safety

objectives.text: Look at different safety tools like Guardrails AI, NeMo Guardrails
Force the LLM to give answers in a strict format and automatically ask again if it gets it wrong using Guardrails AI.
Add checkers to block bad user inputs and stop prompt injection attacks.
Add checkers to stop the LLM from making things up, going off-topic, or leaking private data.
Put strict limits on Agent apps to check tool inputs and stop the agent from getting stuck in endless loops.

modules.outcome: Check and fix inputs and outputs to make sure the LLM app is safe and reliable before users see the results.

modules.name: Application serving & containerization

objectives.text: Move the app logic from simple scripts into a strong, real-world FastAPI backend.
Turn Streamlit into just a screen that talks to the FastAPI backend.
Send answers word-by-word in real time (streaming) so users do not have to wait for the whole reply.
Create an application frontend using Streamlit which handles user queries
Pack the frontend and backend into Docker containers and connect them using Docker Compose.
Hide passwords and API keys safely inside the containers using .env files.

modules.outcome: Upgrade the apps into a fast, streaming, and easily movable container setup.

modules.name: CI/CD with GitHub Actions

objectives.text: Build automatic pipelines in GitHub Actions that use your tests as a strict door to production.
Run the DeepEval tests automatically every time you push new code.
Stop the release instantly if any test score falls below your set limits.
Build effective gates to apply regression testing on new versions
Build Docker images with clear version tags only after all tests pass.
Upload the safe and tested Docker images to Docker Hub.

modules.outcome: Automate your testing and building steps so only high-quality code goes live.

modules.name: Deployment on AWS

objectives.text: Set up AWS EC2 servers to run LLM workloads, installing Docker and the right access roles.
Automate the release process using AWS CodeDeploy to pull new Docker images and swap them safely.
Set up a Load Balancer to manage traffic and make sure the word-by-word streaming works smoothly.
Add Auto Scaling to automatically add more servers when busy and remove them when quiet.
Store sensitive API keys securely in the cloud using AWS Secrets Manager.

Compare this self-managed path with deploying the same app against a managed platform such as Bedrock, Vertex AI, or Azure AI Foundry, where identity, networking, and the model endpoint are provided for you.
Plan capacity on a managed platform: request quota increases, choose between on-demand and provisioned throughput, and watch the token limits that throttle you before your servers do.

modules.outcome: Launch your packed apps on AWS with automatic updates, traffic management, and scaling.

modules.name: Post-deployment monitoring

objectives.text: Set up Prometheus on a special server to gather health data from all your running machines.
Watch computer health stats like CPU, memory, and network usage using Node Exporter.
Track app stats like the number of requests, LLM calls, and tokens used.
Build simple Grafana dashboards to see the health of your servers, app traffic, and LLM behavior in one place.
Set up alarms in Grafana to warn you if servers get too busy or fail to scale.
Monitor logs, latency and token costs for each of your inputs through tracing.
Run frequent online evaluations over your app.

modules.outcome: Keep a close watch on your live AWS setup, covering both the computer health and app speed.

modules.name: Capstone: LLMOps Project

objectives.text: Choose an Agent app and show off the whole LLMOps process from start to finish.
Build around core LLMOps steps: app building, tracking settings, automatic testing, live watching, safety checkers, Docker packing, auto-releases, AWS hosting, and Grafana dashboards.
For this project, follow the path: build →  test → track → secure → pack → launch → watch.

modules.outcome: Show a fully launched, watched, and safe Agent app built from the ground up.

completionOutcomes: Build LLM apps and move them into real-world container setups.
Manage different prompt versions and track settings easily.
Test RAG and Agent apps thoroughly without needing perfect human answers.
Force exact output formats and block bad inputs or data leaks.
Make automatic pipelines that test your app before letting it go live.
Launch, balance traffic, and automatically grow your LLM servers on AWS.
Watch your instance health, app speed, and LLM costs continuously in the real world.

levels.title: Managed AI Platforms
levels.scope: Ship an AI application on the platforms teams actually buy — a cloud provider's managed platform, an open-weight hosting provider, or a router spanning several — and know which parts to hand over and which to keep.

modules.name: The three ways to consume a model

objectives.text: Understand the three paths an organization can take: a provider's public API, a managed platform inside its own cloud account, or open weights it hosts itself or through an inference provider.
Recognize that open weights no longer imply operating GPUs, since managed platforms and inference providers serve the same open models on demand.
Understand why most regulated organizations cannot use a public API directly, and why that constraint decides architecture long before quality does.
Compare the three paths on identity, data handling, region, capacity, price per token, operational effort, and how quickly new models reach you.
Understand where a managed platform sits relative to the model gateway pattern: it can be your gateway, sit behind one, or be one provider among several that a gateway routes to.

modules.tryIt: Take an application you have already built against a public API and list every component that would change if the same app had to run inside a cloud account.
modules.mentalModel: One application, three consumption paths → public API · managed platform in your cloud · open weights you or a provider host
modules.outcome: Place any AI workload on the right consumption path and defend the choice with reasons other than familiarity.

modules.name: Platform anatomy: Bedrock, Vertex AI & Azure AI Foundry

objectives.text: Understand the shape all three share: a catalog of closed and open-weight models, one endpoint style, one identity system, one network boundary, and one bill.
objectives.group: What a managed platform gives you

objectives.text: Read a platform's model catalog the way you read a model card, noting which providers are offered, which regions carry them, and which versions are pinned or retired.
objectives.group: What a managed platform gives you

objectives.text: Understand how invocation differs from a provider SDK, including the platform's own request format, its converse-style unified API, and the provider-native passthrough where one exists.
objectives.group: What a managed platform gives you

objectives.text: Recognize the platform-specific vocabulary for the same ideas, so a Bedrock, Vertex AI, or Azure AI Foundry document reads as a variation rather than a new subject.
objectives.group: What a managed platform gives you

objectives.text: Call a hosted model on one platform from application code and confirm the response, usage, and cost reporting you get back.
Compare the same prompt across two models in the same catalog without changing how you authenticate, network, or bill.
Understand what the platform does not give you: prompt quality, retrieval design, evaluation depth, and product behavior remain yours.

modules.tryIt: Run one prompt against a closed model and an open-weight model in the same catalog, and compare quality, latency, and price per thousand tokens.
modules.outcome: Work confidently on at least one managed platform and map its concepts onto the other two.

modules.name: Identity, networking & tenancy

objectives.text: Replace API keys with cloud identity: roles, service accounts, and workload identity that grant a service the right to invoke a model.
Apply least privilege to model access, scoping which models, regions, and actions an application or team may use.
Understand how platform access is audited, and why an audit trail of who invoked which model matters in regulated environments.
Reach a model over private connectivity so requests never traverse the public internet, and understand what that buys you and what it costs.
Design tenant isolation on a shared platform: separate accounts or projects, scoped credentials, per-tenant keys, and retrieval that cannot cross a tenant boundary.
Understand encryption and key management options, including customer-managed keys for data at rest.

modules.tryIt: Invoke a model from a private network path with no public egress, then verify from the logs that the request never left the account.
modules.outcome: Deploy an AI workload whose identity, network path, and tenant boundaries would survive a security review.

modules.name: Regions, residency & compliance

objectives.text: Understand that a model exists in specific regions, and that the region you are permitted to use often decides which models you may design around.
Plan for data residency requirements, including Indian data-localization expectations and the sector rules that sit above them.
Understand retention and training terms in writing: what the platform logs, for how long, who can see it, and whether your data may be used to improve a model.
Connect these controls to the governance work of Level 8, where residency, deletion, and third-party processing were named as requirements.
Handle the common case where the model you want is unavailable in your required region, through cross-region reasoning, a different model, or an exception you can document.

modules.outcome: State, for a given workload, exactly where the data goes, where it is processed, how long it is kept, and under whose terms.

modules.name: Capacity, quotas & cost

objectives.text: Distinguish on-demand capacity from provisioned or reserved throughput, and understand why committed capacity changes both price and rate limits.
Read the quota model of a platform: requests per minute, tokens per minute, concurrent requests, and per-model limits that differ by region.
Plan for burst traffic with queueing, backpressure, and batch endpoints instead of assuming the platform will absorb a spike.
Request and defend a quota increase with traffic evidence, since capacity is an approval process rather than a setting.
Model cost per request end to end, including input and output tokens, retrieval calls, and any managed component you invoke along the way.
Attribute cost to a project, team, or tenant using the platform's own tagging and billing views, which a shared API key cannot do.
Set budgets and alerts so a runaway agent loop is caught by spend monitoring rather than by the monthly invoice.
Compare on-demand, committed, and self-hosted economics at your actual volume rather than at the volume in the pricing example.

modules.tryIt: Take a week of real traffic and price it three ways: on-demand, committed capacity, and open weights on your own inference.
modules.outcome: Size capacity and forecast spend for a real workload, and know at what volume each pricing model wins.

modules.name: Open-weight model platforms

objectives.text: Understand the spectrum between calling an API and operating hardware: model hubs, serverless inference providers, GPU compute platforms, and your own servers.
Use a model hub such as Hugging Face to find open-weight models, read their cards, check licences and gated access, and judge whether a checkpoint is trustworthy.
Call an open-weight model through a serverless inference provider such as Together, Fireworks, Groq, or Replicate, where you pay per token and never see a GPU.
Understand what a GPU compute platform such as Modal, Baseten, or RunPod adds: you bring the serving stack and they schedule, scale, and bill the hardware.
Serve a model yourself with vLLM, TGI, or Ollama, and understand continuous batching, KV-cache reuse, and why a naive request loop wastes most of a GPU.
Compare per-token pricing with per-GPU-hour pricing, and find the utilization point at which renting hardware becomes cheaper than paying per token.
objectives.group: Choosing and paying for open-weight serving

objectives.text: Understand cold starts and scale-to-zero, and why a deployment that idles cheaply may answer its first request slowly.
objectives.group: Choosing and paying for open-weight serving

objectives.text: Size hardware for a model from parameter count, precision, quantization, and KV-cache growth with context length, since memory decides which GPU you need.
objectives.group: Choosing and paying for open-weight serving

objectives.text: Understand what hosting open weights gives you — predictable cost at volume, data that never leaves your boundary, and full control of versions — and what it asks of you in return.
objectives.group: Choosing and paying for open-weight serving

objectives.text: Evaluate an open-weight model against a closed one on your own task before assuming that either is obviously better.
objectives.group: Choosing and paying for open-weight serving

modules.tryIt: Serve one small open-weight model three ways — a serverless provider, a GPU platform, and locally — and compare setup effort, latency, and the cost of a thousand requests.
modules.mentalModel: Open weights are a ladder: someone else's API → someone else's GPUs → your GPUs
modules.outcome: Run an open-weight model on the right rung of the hosting ladder and justify the choice on cost, latency, control, and effort.

modules.name: Model routers & LLM gateways

objectives.text: Understand a gateway as one endpoint in front of many providers: it holds the credentials, accepts one request format, and hides which model actually served the request.
Compare hosted routers such as OpenRouter and Portkey with self-hosted proxies such as LiteLLM, and with the routing built into cloud platforms and framework gateways.
Route by rule — task type, cost ceiling, context length, latency target, region, or risk — and fail over automatically when a provider errors or throttles.
Use a gateway's spend controls: virtual keys per team or per feature, budgets, quotas, and per-key rate limits that stop one client exhausting shared capacity.
Get one view of usage, latency, errors, and cost across every provider instead of stitching separate dashboards together.
Understand the failure mode you have introduced, since a gateway now sits on the critical path and needs its own availability, timeouts, and a bypass plan.
Handle the provider differences a gateway cannot hide: tool-calling formats, structured-output support, token limits, and prompts that behave differently on each model.
Cache at the gateway, both exact-match and semantic, and decide which requests must never be answered from a cache.
Decide when a router earns its place — several providers, several teams, or spend worth governing — and when one provider and a client library is the honest answer.
Keep evals in the loop, because a routing rule change swaps the model answering your users without a single line of application code changing.

modules.tryIt: Put a router in front of two providers, force the primary to fail, and confirm the fallback answers inside your latency budget.
modules.outcome: Run model traffic through a router that gives you failover, spend control, and one view of usage, without pretending that providers are interchangeable.

modules.name: Managed building blocks: build or buy

objectives.text: Understand managed retrieval offerings such as knowledge bases and enterprise search, which package ingestion, chunking, embedding, and retrieval behind a configuration.
Compare a managed knowledge base with the retrieval stack you built in Level 4 on control over chunking, retrieval tuning, evaluation depth, and cost at your corpus size.
Understand managed agent and workflow runtimes, and what they assume about tools, memory, and orchestration compared with the agents you built in Level 5.
Understand managed guardrails for content filtering, topic restriction, and sensitive-data redaction, and where they sit relative to your own checks.
Understand managed evaluation offerings and judge whether their metrics answer the questions your eval suite from Level 7 was built to answer.
Understand managed fine-tuning and distillation, including which base models can be adapted, where the resulting weights live, and whether you can take them with you.
Decide each layer separately, since adopting a managed retrieval service does not commit you to managed agents, guardrails, or evaluation.
Judge each candidate on control, transparency, evaluation depth, cost at your volume, and how much of the behavior you must be able to explain to an auditor.
Measure the portability cost before adopting: a prompt moves between providers in minutes, while a knowledge base, agent, or guardrail configuration usually does not.
Recognize the honest cases for buying: a small team, a standard use case, a compliance deadline, or a workload whose quality bar the managed component already clears.

modules.tryIt: Rebuild one component of an existing application on a managed equivalent, then compare quality, cost, and how much control you gave up.
modules.mentalModel: Buy the plumbing you cannot differentiate on, build the layer your product is judged by
modules.outcome: Make a defensible build-or-buy call for every layer of an AI system instead of adopting or rejecting managed services wholesale.

modules.name: Portability, lock-in & migration

objectives.text: Separate what is portable from what is not: prompts, evals, and application code travel easily, while managed indexes, agent definitions, and platform-specific APIs do not.
Keep an abstraction between application code and provider so a model swap is a configuration change rather than a rewrite.
Understand the real costs of lock-in beyond price: model availability, feature pace, negotiating position, and the work of proving a new platform is safe.
Plan a migration between platforms or providers as an evaluation exercise, re-running your eval suite before, during, and after the move.
Handle catalog lag and platform-side deprecation, since managed catalogs trail the frontier and retire versions on their own schedule.
Run two platforms in parallel where the workload justifies it, using a gateway to route by capability, region, cost, or availability.
Understand multi-cloud honestly: it buys resilience and leverage, and it costs duplicated evaluation, duplicated security review, and duplicated operational knowledge.

modules.outcome: Adopt a platform without being trapped by it, and move a workload between platforms without discovering the coupling too late.

modules.name: Capstone: deploy on a managed platform

objectives.text: Take an application you built in an earlier level and redeploy it against a managed platform, keeping the behavior and changing the plumbing.
Authenticate through cloud identity with least-privilege access to a named set of models, and remove the provider API key from the application entirely.
Route model traffic over a private network path, and record where the data is processed, how long it is retained, and under which terms.
Replace at least one hand-built component with a managed equivalent, and keep at least one hand-built because you can defend why.
Re-run your evaluation suite on the migrated system and report what changed in quality, latency, and cost.
Route the application's model calls through a gateway with a working fallback, or state why direct calls to one provider are enough at your scale.
Size capacity for your expected traffic, set a budget alert, and state the volume at which a different pricing model would win.
Write a one-page platform decision record: the workload, the constraints, the path chosen, the components bought and built, and the exit plan.

modules.finalResult: the same application, running where a regulated employer could actually run it, with the identity, network, residency, capacity, cost, and portability decisions written down.

completionOutcomes: Place a workload on the right consumption path among a public API, a managed platform, and open weights you or a provider host.
Work on at least one managed platform and read the other two as variations rather than new subjects.
Replace API keys with cloud identity and scope model access with least privilege.
Reach a model over a private network path and explain what that guarantees.
Isolate tenants on shared infrastructure, including retrieval that cannot cross a tenant boundary.
State where data is processed, how long it is retained, and whether it may be used for training.
Plan around regional model availability and data-residency requirements.
Size on-demand versus provisioned capacity and defend a quota increase with traffic evidence.
Attribute spend per project, team, or tenant, and catch runaway cost with budgets and alerts.
Place an open-weight model on the right rung of the hosting ladder, from a serverless provider to your own GPUs.
Compare per-token and per-GPU-hour economics and find the volume at which each one wins.
Run model traffic through a router with failover, spend controls, and one view of usage across providers.
Decide build or buy for retrieval, agents, guardrails, evaluation, and fine-tuning, layer by layer.
Measure the portability cost of a managed component before adopting it.
Migrate a workload between platforms with your eval suite as the safety net.
Deploy an existing application inside a cloud account in a form a regulated employer could accept.

levels.title: Multimodal 101: Beyond Text
levels.scope: Build a strong mental model of how models handle images, audio, and video, why they fail differently from text models, and how to choose and use the right model when a task stops being text-only.

modules.name: Beyond text: what a multimodal model is

objectives.text: Understand what makes a model multimodal: images, audio, and video are converted into tokens and fed into the same transformer that already processes text.
Distinguish a natively multimodal model, trained on mixed data from the start, from a pipeline that bolts a separate transcription, OCR, or captioning model in front of a text-only LLM.
Understand why text remains the interlingua: whatever enters the model, the reasoning and almost always the output happen in tokens that behave like text.
Build intuition for what changes and what does not: the context window, tokenization, sampling, and failure modes you learned for text all still apply.
Recognize what "any-to-any" marketing does and does not mean today, since most models accept several input modalities but produce only text.
Understand why a bolted-on pipeline loses information that a native model keeps, such as tone in speech or layout in a scanned page.

modules.tryIt: Send the same chart as an image to a natively multimodal model and as OCR-extracted text to a text-only model, then compare what each one can answer.
modules.mentalModel: Image / audio / video → tokens → the same transformer you already understand → text out
modules.outcome: Explain to someone what a multimodal model actually is, and tell whether a given product is using a native model or a pipeline stitched together around a text model.

modules.name: Vision: how images become tokens

objectives.text: Understand how a vision encoder splits an image into a grid of patches and turns each patch into a vector the transformer can consume.
Build intuition for why a single image can cost hundreds or thousands of tokens, and why that cost scales with resolution rather than with file size.
Understand tiling and detail settings: high-detail modes slice a large image into multiple tiles, each priced as its own set of tokens.
Recognize what downscaling and aspect-ratio changes destroy, especially small text, thin lines, dense tables, and fine chart labels.
Understand that image tokens occupy the same context window as text tokens, so a handful of screenshots can crowd out the instructions and history around them.
Understand the practical trade-off between sending one large detailed image, several cropped regions, or a downscaled overview.

modules.tryIt: Send the same screenshot at full resolution, at half resolution, and cropped to the region that matters, then compare token usage, cost, and answer quality.
modules.outcome: Predict roughly what an image will cost in tokens and choose a resolution and cropping strategy instead of uploading whatever the camera produced.

modules.name: Vision: capabilities & failure modes

objectives.text: Understand what vision models genuinely do well: reading text in images, describing scenes, extracting named fields from documents, and interpreting charts at a coarse level.
Understand the failure modes that repeat across models: precise counting, spatial and geometric reasoning, dense small text, and exact row-to-column alignment in tables.
Recognize fabricated detail, where a model confidently reports values, labels, or objects that a low-resolution or ambiguous image never actually contained.
Understand why these failures happen: the model is generating a plausible description of an image it perceives as patches, not measuring or verifying anything.
Adopt the engineering question for vision too: not "can this model read invoices?", but "how reliably does it read my invoices, at my resolution, in my formats?".
Understand which safeguards apply when reliability is not enough, such as higher resolution, cropping, structured output, verification passes, or human review.

modules.tryIt: Build ten test images that include a crowded shelf, a dense table, a low-resolution receipt, and a handwritten note, then score how often the model is exactly right.
modules.outcome: Predict which visual tasks a model will handle unaided and which need cropping, higher resolution, or a verification step before you can ship them.

modules.name: Vision: documents, charts & visual RAG

objectives.text: Distinguish a digital PDF that carries its own text layer from a scan or photograph where every character has to be recovered from pixels.
objectives.group: Reading a document as an image

objectives.text: Compare OCR-based reading with native vision reading by a multimodal model on accuracy, cost, latency, and how much layout they preserve.
objectives.group: Reading a document as an image

objectives.text: Understand why reading order matters: multi-column pages, headers, footers, footnotes, and sidebars can turn a correct page into nonsense when flattened badly.
objectives.group: Reading a document as an image

objectives.text: Read tables and forms reliably, including merged cells, multi-page tables, checkboxes, and key-value layouts where the label and the value sit far apart.
objectives.group: Reading a document as an image

objectives.text: Understand what a model actually does with a chart: it reads axes, labels, and legends rather than the underlying numbers, so precise values are often estimated.
objectives.group: Reading a document as an image

objectives.text: Define the schema before the prompt: name the fields you need, their types, and which of them are required, instead of asking for a free-form summary.
Extract fields from a document with a vision model and validate the result against that schema, checking types, ranges, dates, totals, and required values.
Ground every extracted field in its source by returning the page number or region it came from, so a human can verify a value without rereading the document.
Recognize document-specific failure modes: invented values in blank cells, rows merged across page breaks, confused units or currencies, and misread handwriting.
Route low-confidence extractions to human review rather than letting an uncertain value flow silently into a database.
Understand what changes when the retrieval unit is a page image or a region of a page rather than a chunk of text, and how embeddings are produced for it.
Build hybrid retrieval that searches extracted text and page images together, and recognize which of the two wins for a given question.
Cite the page or region an answer came from, so the reader can open the document at the right place and check it.
Compare a visual pipeline with a plain text pipeline on cost, latency, and accuracy, and understand why clean digital text rarely needs page images at all.
Understand the practical cost of visual RAG: page images consume far more tokens than the equivalent text, which changes both latency and price per query.

modules.tryIt: Take one scanned invoice and one clean digital PDF, run both through a text pipeline and a vision pipeline, and compare accuracy, cost, and latency.
modules.mentalModel: Document → Pages → Text layer + page images → Layout & regions → Structured fields or retrievable units
modules.outcome: Build a document pipeline that reads real-world PDFs and scans, extracts validated fields, and answers questions with a citation back to the page it used.

modules.name: Vision: image & video generation

objectives.text: Understand that a generative image model starts from random noise and repeatedly removes it, rather than predicting the next token the way an LLM does.
Understand what a prompt actually controls in image generation: subject, composition, style, and detail, with far less literal instruction-following than a text model offers.
Understand seeds and reproducibility: the same prompt with the same seed returns the same image, while a new seed produces a different interpretation of the same words.
Understand how resolution, aspect ratio, and step count affect quality, generation time, and cost.
Distinguish text-to-image from image-to-image, inpainting, and outpainting, and recognize which one a given editing task actually needs.
Understand reference and style conditioning, along with structural control such as pose, depth, or edge guidance, for when a prompt alone cannot hold a layout steady.
Build intuition for iteration cost: generation is cheap per image but expensive per accepted image, because most candidates are discarded.
Understand what video generation adds: time, motion, and consistency across frames, which makes length, cost, and failure modes grow quickly.
Understand provenance and rights: watermarking, content credentials, training-data licensing, and the commercial-use terms attached to generated assets.

modules.tryIt: Generate the same prompt at three seeds and three aspect ratios, then edit the best result with inpainting instead of re-prompting it.
modules.mentalModel: Noise → repeated denoising guided by the prompt → image
modules.outcome: Produce and iteratively control generated images, and judge whether a generation task is worth its cost in review time and rights risk.

modules.name: Audio: how sound becomes tokens

objectives.text: Understand the path from a waveform to model input: audio is sampled, converted into a spectrogram or learned audio tokens, and then treated as another token stream.
Build intuition for audio cost and latency, where tokens accumulate per second of duration rather than per word, so silence and background noise are paid for too.
Distinguish transcribe-then-prompt pipelines, where a speech-to-text model produces text for an LLM, from audio-native models that consume the sound itself.
Understand what a transcript discards: tone, emphasis, hesitation, overlapping speakers, emotion, and everything that separates "fine" said warmly from "fine" said flatly.
Recognize why audio input and output are latency-sensitive, since a conversation is judged on response delay in a way that a document summary never is.
Understand common audio failure modes such as accented speech, code-switching between languages, domain jargon, poor microphones, and long silences.

modules.tryIt: Run the same 30-second clip through a speech-to-text model and through an audio-native model, and ask both what the speaker's mood was.
modules.outcome: Choose between a transcription pipeline and an audio-native model for a given task, and explain what each choice costs you in fidelity, latency, and money.

modules.name: Audio: speech to text & text to speech

objectives.text: Understand what a speech-to-text model such as Whisper produces: a transcript, optional word timestamps, and confidence signals rather than clean edited prose.
Distinguish batch transcription of a complete recording from streaming transcription, where partial text is emitted while the speaker is still talking.
Understand what degrades transcription in practice — accents, code-mixed Hindi-English speech, background noise, and poor microphones — and supply domain vocabulary as hints.
Use speaker diarization to attribute each segment to a speaker, and understand why it is a separate step that fails in its own ways.
Read word error rate as a measure of transcription quality, and reason about which errors actually matter for whatever happens downstream.
Understand what a text-to-speech model such as Kokoro turns text into: sampled audio in a chosen voice, produced in one pass or streamed as it is generated.
Choose a voice and shape prosody through pace, pauses, and emphasis, and understand how much control a given model actually exposes.
Control the pronunciation of names, acronyms, numbers, and code-mixed text, since these are where synthetic speech usually embarrasses itself.
Stream synthesis so the first audio reaches the listener while the rest is still being generated, instead of waiting for the whole utterance.
Compare hosted and locally run speech models on cost, latency, privacy, and voice quality, and choose per workload rather than by default.

modules.tryIt: Transcribe a five-minute recording that mixes Hindi and English, then read the transcript back with a synthetic voice and note where each step breaks.
modules.mentalModel: Audio → Transcript + timestamps + speakers → Text → Synthesized audio
modules.outcome: Build a speech pipeline that transcribes real recordings and speaks generated text back, with a clear view of where accuracy and latency are lost.

modules.name: Audio: realtime voice agents

objectives.text: Understand why a voice conversation feels broken above roughly a second of silence, and treat end-to-end latency as the primary design constraint.
Break the latency budget into its parts: capture, network, transcription, model thinking, synthesis, and playback.
Distinguish a cascaded pipeline, where speech-to-text, an LLM, and text-to-speech run in sequence, from a speech-to-speech realtime API that takes audio in and returns audio.
Compare the two architectures on latency, control, cost, debuggability, and how much of the conversation you can inspect afterwards.
Understand which parts can overlap: synthesis can begin before the model has finished, and transcription can run while the user is still speaking.
Understand voice activity detection and endpointing as the mechanism that decides when the user has actually stopped speaking.
Recognize why endpointing is hard: pauses for thought, slow speakers, and background chatter all look like the end of a turn.
Handle barge-in, where the user interrupts mid-answer, by stopping playback and discarding the rest of the planned response.
Use partial transcripts to start work early, and understand the risk of acting on text the user has not finished saying.
Keep conversation state consistent when a turn is cut short, so the model does not believe it said something the user never heard.
Handle silence, dead air, and network loss with holding phrases, reconnection, and a graceful exit rather than an unexplained pause.
Understand what background noise, crosstalk, and poor microphones do to a live pipeline, and where to place the safeguards.
Keep the conversation alive while a tool call runs, since a lookup that takes three seconds is silence the user will not tolerate.
Decide what the agent says while it waits, and what it does when the tool fails or returns nothing useful.
Capture what a voice session needs for later reconstruction: audio, transcript, timings, and turn boundaries.

modules.tryIt: Build a small voice loop with speech-to-text, an LLM, and text-to-speech, then measure the delay from the end of your sentence to the first sound of the reply.
modules.mentalModel: User speech → VAD & endpointing → Transcript → Model → Speech, with barge-in resetting the loop
modules.outcome: Ship a voice agent that holds a natural conversation: it knows when you stopped talking, it can be interrupted, and it keeps silence short enough to feel human.

modules.name: Cross-modal search & retrieval

objectives.text: Understand a shared embedding space, where an image and a caption that describe the same thing land close together as vectors.
Understand CLIP-style joint embeddings, where two encoders are trained so that matching image-text pairs are pulled together and mismatched pairs pushed apart.
Search images with a text query and search text with an image query, using the same vector-search machinery Level 4 introduced for text.
Distinguish cross-modal retrieval from captioning every image first and searching the captions, and recognize when each approach wins.
Recognize where cross-modal retrieval fails: fine-grained detail, text inside images, counting, and domain-specific imagery the encoder never saw.
Evaluate retrieval quality on your own images and queries rather than trusting a benchmark score measured on a general image collection.

modules.tryIt: Build a small image index, query it in plain language, and compare the results with a caption-then-search baseline over the same images.
modules.mentalModel: Different modalities → one shared vector space → distance means similarity
modules.outcome: Decide when a task needs cross-modal retrieval and build a small image-and-text search over your own collection.

modules.name: Choosing a multimodal model

objectives.text: Start from the modalities themselves: list what must go in, whether text, images, audio, video, or documents, and what must come out.
Understand how multimodal pricing works, since per-image and per-audio-minute charges sit alongside per-token pricing and cost stops being about text length alone.
Understand the context cost of images, where a single image consumes a large, resolution-dependent share of the context window and limits how many you can pass at once.
Compare latency expectations by modality, including time to first audio for streaming voice, where a delay is heard by the user rather than merely measured.
Weigh API access against self-hosting for vision and speech, where open models are strong and per-minute costs at volume can outgrow the operational effort.
Treat privacy as a harder constraint here, because voices, faces, and scanned documents carry consent and data-residency obligations that plain text often does not.
Consider managed speech, vision, and document services from the cloud platforms alongside general multimodal models, since a narrow managed service is often cheaper and more accurate at one job.
Shortlist two or three candidates, then test them on your own images, recordings, and documents before committing, exactly as you would for a text model.

modules.outcome: Choose a model for a multimodal task on modality support, cost per unit, latency, and privacy, verified against your own examples.

modules.name: Deep research & long-horizon scenarios

objectives.text: Understand what changes when a task runs for many minutes across many sources instead of resolving inside a single prompt and a single response.
Decompose a research question into sub-questions that can be investigated independently, and recognize when a question is too vague to decompose yet.
Search broadly before going deep: gather many candidate sources first, judge which few are worth reading closely, and discard the rest deliberately.
Read sources critically rather than accumulating them, distinguishing primary evidence, secondary commentary, marketing material, and outdated claims.
Reconcile sources that disagree by preferring better evidence, stating the disagreement explicitly, or reporting genuine uncertainty instead of averaging the answers.
Keep every claim attached to the source it came from, so a reader can verify any individual statement without repeating the whole search.
Manage a run that outlives its context by writing notes and interim summaries as the work proceeds, and by carrying forward findings rather than raw source text.
Recognize the stopping conditions of a research run: the question is answered, the sources have started repeating, or the remaining uncertainty cannot be resolved by more searching.
Produce a structured report a human can audit, with the question, the answer, the supporting evidence, the contradictions found, and the gaps that remain.

Understand the characteristic failures of long-horizon runs: drifting away from the original question, confident synthesis of thin evidence, and citations that do not support the sentence attached to them.

modules.tryIt: Run the same research question twice, once with a five-minute budget and once with a thirty-minute budget, and compare what the extra time actually bought.
modules.outcome: Run a long-horizon research task that produces a cited, structured report whose claims a reader can check individually.

modules.name: On-device & edge modalities

objectives.text: Understand why speech and vision suit on-device execution, since the models are small, the input is private, and the network round trip is often the slowest part.
Understand quantization as trading numerical precision for size and speed, and recognize the tasks where that trade shows up first as degraded quality.
Build intuition for hardware limits on phones and laptops, including memory ceilings, thermal throttling, and battery cost during sustained inference.
Understand what on-device execution buys you: offline operation, no per-request cost, predictable latency, and data that never leaves the user's machine.
Choose deliberately between on-device, self-hosted, and API execution for each modality, since one application can reasonably use all three at once.

modules.tryIt: Run a small quantized speech-to-text model locally and compare its accuracy, latency, and cost against a hosted API on the same audio.
modules.outcome: Decide which parts of a multimodal system belong on the user's device and accept the quality trade knowingly.

modules.name: Capstone: ship a multimodal build

objectives.text: Choose one realistic build and take it all the way: a voice agent, a document-understanding pipeline, a visual search tool, or a research-report generator.
Combine at least two modalities in a single application so the build exercises a real cross-modal boundary rather than one model in isolation.
Feed the system real inputs from your own domain, including the messy scans, accented speech, and awkward layouts that curated sample files never contain.
Handle the modality-specific failures your build will actually hit, such as unreadable regions, silence and background noise, hallucinated chart values, or ambiguous references.
Measure latency and cost per request, and report them broken down by modality so the expensive part of the pipeline is visible.
Document one failure you found by testing on real inputs, explaining what broke, how you detected it, and what you changed in response.
Package the build so another person can run it from a README with their own inputs, their own credentials, and no help from you.

modules.finalResult: a working multimodal application that survives real inputs, whose latency and cost you can quote, and whose limitations you can state precisely.

completionOutcomes: Explain how a multimodal model represents images, audio, and text in a single sequence, and why that makes cross-modal reasoning possible.
Predict the token cost of an image, a page, or a minute of audio, and estimate the cost of a multimodal request before sending it.
Choose sensible resolution, cropping, and sampling settings instead of sending every input at maximum fidelity.
Judge which vision tasks a model handles reliably and which ones need verification, structure, or a different tool.
Extract structured data from documents, charts, and tables, and build retrieval over pages that text extraction alone would destroy.
Use image and video generation models with enough control to produce specific outputs rather than plausible ones.
Build a speech-to-text pipeline and a text-to-speech pipeline, and reason about accuracy, latency, and cost across the options available.
Build a realtime voice agent with acceptable turn-taking, interruption handling, and end-to-end latency.
Retrieve across modalities using shared embedding spaces, and understand where cross-modal similarity breaks down.
Select a model per modality on capability, latency, cost, context, and deployment rather than on a single leaderboard position.
Run a long-horizon research task that produces a cited, auditable report instead of a confident summary.
Reason about running models locally, including quantization, memory limits, and the quality you trade away for privacy and offline operation.
Ship a multimodal application that handles real inputs, whose cost and latency you have measured and whose failure modes you can name.

levels.title: Fine-Tuning
levels.scope: the prompt-vs-RAG-vs-fine-tune call, and a small tune when an eval justifies it.

objectives.text: Make the tradeoff honestly; identify the narrow cases where FT wins.
Build and format high-quality training data (most of the real work).
Run a LoRA/QLoRA tune with PEFT (Unsloth/Axolotl) and set hyperparameters.
Build preference data and run DPO; know when it's warranted.
Explain reward-based tuning intuition and its use cases.
Distill a large model into a small one for cost/latency wins.
Measure before/after on Level-7 evals and catch regressions.

modules.name: Capstone: a LoRA that beats a prompted baseline

objectives.text: Ship a tune with the eval numbers, before and after, as proof.

levels.title: Projects
levels.scope: proof, not concepts. Portfolio builds that compose earlier levels. Ship 3–5 public.

objectives.text: Compose L4 with FastAPI and a retrieval eval; deploy publicly.
Demonstrate tool calling and structured output on a real business task.
Show LangGraph orchestration and state management (L5).

modules.name: MCP server for a real tool

objectives.text: Connect a model to a calendar/CRM/task manager — the 2026 pattern.
Tell the ops story: routing, fallback, cost caps, tracing (L10).
Ship a realtime voice agent or a vision pipeline (L12).
Write projects up, publish to GitHub, record demos, and present the work.

levels.title: GenAI / AI Engineer Interview Prep
levels.scope: convert everything learned across the roadmap into interview performance. This level does not re-teach concepts; it focuses on scenario-based questions, system-design discussions, debugging cases, trade-offs, and defending real engineering decisions under interview conditions.

modules.name: Interview strategy & role positioning

objectives.text: Understand how GenAI interviews have shifted from theory-heavy questioning toward system design, debugging, architecture, and production scenarios.
Learn to read a job description and identify which roadmap areas are actually being tested instead of trying to prepare every listed tool.
Distinguish AI Engineer, GenAI Data Scientist, and traditional Data Scientist roles by emphasis rather than treating them as completely separate disciplines.
Understand why modern AI-engineering interviews increasingly emphasize the engineering layer: APIs, inference, LLMOps, observability, networking, cloud, reliability, and deployment.
Practice explaining API-hosted models vs self-hosted open-weight models across capability, cost, latency, control, privacy, and operational burden.
Build a personalized interview-preparation plan based on target role and current weaknesses.

modules.outcome: Prioritize interview preparation intelligently and position your existing skillset for the role being targeted.

modules.name: Production RAG interview scenarios

objectives.text: Design ingestion pipelines for messy enterprise data containing complex PDFs, nested tables, diagrams, varying layouts, and continuously changing documents.
Whiteboard a RAG system serving large numbers of concurrent users across very large document collections.
Separate the architecture into services such as embedding, retrieval, LLM inference, ingestion, orchestration, and storage.
Explain why application/orchestration services should often remain stateless while persistent state belongs in databases, object stores, vector databases, graph databases, caches, or search indexes.
Reason about production infrastructure around RAG:
asynchronous messaging and queues,
service fallbacks,
object/vector/graph/search storage,
observability and SLAs,
networking and IAM,
secrets and encryption,
CI/CD and deployment.
Practice debugging scenarios such as: “The RAG system worked well for a week and then quality dropped. How would you investigate?”
Isolate failures across ingestion, retrieval, generation, data changes, model changes, and infrastructure.

modules.outcome: Whiteboard and defend a production-scale RAG architecture rather than describing a demo-level retriever → LLM pipeline.

modules.name: Agentic AI interview scenarios

objectives.text: Design an agentic system for a concrete business task involving planning, tools, memory, and multi-step execution.
Defend the choice between a deterministic workflow and an autonomous agent.
Reason about tools, MCP integrations, memory, and multi-agent architectures under realistic constraints.
Handle common interview failure scenarios:
runaway loops,
poor tool selection,
tool failures,
nondeterministic trajectories,
excessive token/cost usage,
context degradation,
overly powerful tool permissions.
Design human-in-the-loop checkpoints and guardrails for consequential actions.
Debug an agent from its trajectory when it succeeds in testing but fails under production conditions.
Explain when not to introduce multi-agent or autonomous behavior.

notes: Note: the source marks this session as reconstructed because the original Session 3 transcript was not provided, so these topics are inferred from the series plan rather than directly transcribed.
modules.outcome: Design and defend an agent architecture while reasoning explicitly about autonomy, cost, reliability, recovery, and blast radius.

modules.name: Fine-tuning & model adaptation interviews

objectives.text: Make the prompt vs RAG vs fine-tuning decision from a concrete product brief.
Explain when fine-tuning creates meaningful value and when it adds unnecessary training and deployment complexity.
Discuss LoRA, QLoRA, PEFT, and quantization in terms of engineering trade-offs rather than only definitions.
Reason about deploying a fine-tuned open-weight model: serving architecture, GPU requirements, inference optimization, latency, and cost.
Practice the debugging case: “The fine-tuned model performed well before deployment, but production accuracy dropped. What do you investigate?”
Consider training data, formatting, distribution shift, evaluation regressions, inference configuration, serving changes, and quantization artifacts.

modules.outcome: Defend a model-adaptation strategy and systematically debug performance degradation after deployment.

modules.name: LLMOps & production debugging interviews

objectives.text: Diagnose production incidents involving model APIs, self-hosted inference, retrieval services, queues, caches, rate limits, and downstream tools.
Reason through latency spikes, provider outages, cost explosions, capacity limits, and degraded model quality.
Discuss fallback strategies, graceful degradation, retries, load balancing, and autoscaling.
Interpret monitoring signals such as latency, throughput, error rates, token usage, cost, retrieval quality, and eval scores.
Explain what should trigger an alert and what requires rollback versus investigation.
Practice comparing proprietary API deployment with self-hosted inference under realistic traffic and privacy constraints.

modules.outcome: Demonstrate that you can operate and troubleshoot an AI system after it leaves the notebook.

modules.name: AI system-design interviews

objectives.text: Practice turning an ambiguous product requirement into explicit assumptions around users, traffic, latency, quality, cost, freshness, privacy, and reliability.
Start with the simplest viable architecture before introducing RAG, agents, fine-tuning, routing, caching, or complex infrastructure.
Whiteboard systems using the full AI stack:
model selection/routing,
RAG and context,
tools/agents,
caches,
databases,
inference services,
observability,
evals,
security,
deployment.
Design under enterprise constraints where a public API is not allowed, and defend a managed platform or self-hosted deployment on identity, residency, capacity, and cost.
Explain every major trade-off rather than merely naming technologies.
Practice system designs such as:
enterprise support assistant,
coding assistant,
research agent,
large-scale document intelligence system.

modules.outcome: Run a structured AI-system-design interview from requirements through architecture, bottlenecks, failure modes, and scaling.

modules.name: Staying current without chasing hype

objectives.text: Build a defensible process for evaluating new models, frameworks, papers, benchmarks, and tooling.
Separate meaningful capability/infrastructure changes from short-lived hype.
Explain how you would evaluate a newly released model before replacing an existing production model.
Use benchmarks → shortlist → custom evals → cost/latency comparison → controlled rollout rather than social-media consensus.
Develop a strong answer to common interview questions such as “How do you stay current in GenAI?”

notes: This reflects the source’s intended “GenAI philosophy” component, though that final session was also reconstructed because its transcript was unavailable.
modules.outcome: Demonstrate informed judgment rather than simply listing the latest tools.

modules.name: Project & portfolio defense

objectives.text: Prepare 2–3 major projects from the roadmap for deep technical questioning.
Explain each project using:
problem → requirements → baseline → architecture → decisions → trade-offs → failures → evals → production results.
Be prepared to explain why you selected a particular model, retriever, agent architecture, framework, database, or deployment strategy.
Quantify where possible: quality scores, latency, cost/query, throughput, dataset size, traffic, or improvement over baseline.
Discuss failures and design mistakes openly and explain what you changed as a result.
Prepare for interviewer follow-ups such as:
“Why didn't you use RAG?”
“Why not fine-tune?”
“Why do you need an agent?”
“What happens at 100× traffic?”
“How would you reduce the cost by 50%?”
“What breaks first?”

modules.outcome: Defend projects as engineering decisions rather than merely demonstrate that they work.

modules.name: Behavioral communication for AI engineers

objectives.text: Communicate technical reasoning clearly without drowning the interviewer in implementation details.
State assumptions before solving ambiguous design questions.
Think in structured trade-offs rather than jumping directly to a tool or architecture.
Use diagrams and whiteboards to progressively reveal a design.
When unsure, explain how you would measure, experiment, or debug rather than bluffing.
Structure experience-based answers around the situation, decision, implementation, result, and lessons learned.

modules.outcome: Make strong technical thinking visible to the interviewer.

modules.name: Capstone: Full Mock GenAI Interview Loop

objectives.text: Simulate a complete AI-engineering interview.
Round 1 · Scenario & debugging
Solve rapid production scenarios such as:
RAG accuracy suddenly drops.
Agent enters an expensive loop.
Model provider latency doubles.
Fine-tuned model regresses after deployment.
Prompt change improves quality but doubles cost.
Retriever works offline but fails on real production queries.
Round 2 · System design
Receive an ambiguous product brief and:

Clarify requirements → define constraints → establish baseline → design architecture → choose models → design data/context layer → handle scale → add reliability/security → define evals/monitoring → defend trade-offs.
Round 3 · Project defense
Present one major portfolio project and handle increasingly deep follow-up questions on architecture, alternatives, costs, failures, evals, and scaling.

modules.finalResult: demonstrate that you can reason like an AI engineer under interview conditions, not merely recall AI concepts.
